### 🐛 Describe the bug ## Summary LMCache prefill/decode disaggregation returns incorrect generation results after an apparently successful remote KV-cache transfer. The prefill and decode servers both: - Start successfully. - Return HTTP 200. - Remain healthy after the requests. - Report that LMCache P/D mode is enabled. - Report that the NIXL/UCX transfer channel is active. - Report complete prompt KV-cache hits on the decode receiver. Despite this, the P/D generation diverges from an equivalent monolithic vLLM server starting at generated token 0. The incorrect output frequently begins by reproducing tokens from inside the repeated prompt body: ```text alpha beta gamma delta epsilon zeta eta theta ... ``` The monolithic server instead begins answering the instruction at the end of the prompt: ```text The problem is to summarize the operational sequence ... ``` This is a silent correctness failure. It is not a startup failure, HTTP failure, missing-transfer failure, or unhealthy-engine failure. The issue was reproduced locally: - 6/6 comparisons failed across two independent vLLM 0.26.0 runs. - 3/3 comparisons failed in a separate vLLM 0.27.1 run. - Total: 9/9 LMCache P/D versus monolithic comparisons failed. - Native NIXL and Mooncake passed the identical monolithic-equivalence oracle. ## Environment Primary reproduction environment: ```text OS: Ubuntu 22.04.5 LTS (x86_64) CPU: AMD EPYC 9554 64-Core Processor GPU: NVIDIA L40S Prefill: 1 × L40S Decode: 1 × independent L40S NVIDIA driver: 595.71.05 Python: 3.12.13 vLLM: 0.26.0 LMCache: 0.5.3-g140819c9 NIXL: 1.3.2 PyTorch: 2.11.0+cu130 Transformers: 5.14.1 Model: Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B Model dtype: bfloat16 KV-cache dtype: bfloat16 Tensor parallel size: 1 Execution mode: eager Transfer channel: NIXL NIXL backend: UCX ``` The same failure was independently reproduced with: ```text Python: 3.12.13 vLLM: 0.27.1 LMCache: 0.5.3-g140819c9 NIXL: 1.3.2 PyTorch: 2.13.0 Transformers: 5.15.0 Model: Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B GPU: NVIDIA L40S Model dtype: bfloat16 KV-cache dtype: bfloat16 Tensor parallel size: 1 Execution mode: eager ``` ## LMCache prefill configuration Save as `lmcache_prefill.yaml`: ```yaml local_cpu: false max_local_cpu_size: 0 remote_serde: null enable_pd: true transfer_channel: "nixl" pd_role: "sender" pd_buffer_size: 1073741824 pd_buffer_device: "cuda" nixl_backends: [UCX] pd_proxy_host: "127.0.0.1" pd_proxy_port: 37413 pd_skip_proxy_notification: true ``` ## LMCache decode configuration Save as `lmcache_decode.yaml`: ```yaml local_cpu: false max_local_cpu_size: 0 remote_serde: null enable_pd: true transfer_channel: "nixl" pd_role: "receiver" pd_buffer_size: 1073741824 pd_buffer_device: "cuda" nixl_backends: [UCX] pd_peer_host: "127.0.0.1" pd_peer_init_port: [37413] pd_peer_alloc_port: [42727] ``` The exact port numbers can be replaced with any two unused local ports. The values above are taken from one representative reproduction. ## Common environment variables Run the following before starting the servers: ```bash export LMCACHE_USE_EXPERIMENTAL=True export PYTHONHASHSEED=123 export UCX_TLS=cuda_ipc,cuda_copy,tcp export VLLM_ENABLE_V1_MULTIPROCESSING=1 export VLLM_WORKER_MULTIPROC_METHOD=spawn export VLLM_USE_FLASHINFER_SAMPLER=0 ``` ## Start the prefill server ```bash CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=0 \ LMCACHE_CONFIG_FILE="$PWD/lmcache_prefill.yaml" \ python -m vllm.entrypoints.openai.api_server \ --model Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B \ --served-model-name veritas-model \ --host 127.0.0.1 \ --port 8100 \ --dtype bfloat16 \ --max-model-len 2048 \ --max-num-seqs 8 \ --gpu-memory-utilization 0.65 \ --no-enable-prefix-caching \ --disable-log-stats \ --enforce-eager \ --kv-transfer-config '{"kv_connector":"LMCacheConnectorV1","kv_role":"kv_producer","kv_connector_extra_config":{"discard_partial_chunks":false,"lmcache_rpc_port":"veritas-prefill"}}' ``` Wait until `GET /v1/models` returns HTTP 200. ## Start the decode server ```bash CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=1 \ LMCACHE_CONFIG_FILE="$PWD/lmcache_decode.yaml" \ python -m vllm.entrypoints.openai.api_server \ --model Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B \ --served-model-name veritas-model \ --host 127.0.0.1 \ --port 8200 \ --dtype bfloat16 \ --max-model-len 2048 \ --max-num-seqs 8 \ --gpu-memory-utilization 0.65 \ --no-enable-prefix-caching \ --disable-log-stats \ --enforce-eager \ --kv-transfer-config '{"kv_connector":"LMCacheConnectorV1","kv_role":"kv_consumer","kv_connector_extra_config":{"discard_partial_chunks":false,"lmcache_rpc_port":"veritas-decode"}}' ``` Wait until `GET /v1/models` returns HTTP 200. ## Input Three independent prompts are generated. Each prompt contains a unique random request marker to prevent accidental reuse between repetitions. ```python import uuid repeat = 0 marker = f"VERITAS_PD_{repeat}_{uuid.uuid4().hex[:12]}" prompt = ( f"Request marker {marker}. " + "alpha beta gamma delta epsilon zeta eta theta " * 96 + " Summarize the operational sequence in exactly three short bullets." ) request_id = f"veritas-pd-{repeat}-{uuid.uuid4().hex}" ``` Depending on how the random marker is tokenized, the complete prompt contains approximately 895–898 tokens. The same exact `prompt` and `request_id` are used for the corresponding prefill and decode requests. ## Prefill request ```python import requests prefill_payload = { "model": "veritas-model", "prompt": prompt, "temperature": 0.0, "stream": False, "max_tokens": 1, "kv_transfer_params": { "disagg_spec": { "req_id": request_id, "receiver_host": "127.0.0.1", "receiver_init_port": [37413], "receiver_alloc_port": [42727], } }, } prefill_response = requests.post( "http://127.0.0.1:8100/v1/completions", json=prefill_payload, headers={"X-Request-Id": request_id}, timeout=180, ) print("prefill status:", prefill_response.status_code) print("prefill body:", prefill_response.text) ``` Observed result: ```text prefill status: 200 ``` ## Decode request After the prefill request finishes, send the same prompt and request ID to the decode receiver: ```python decode_payload = { "model": "veritas-model", "prompt": prompt, "temperature": 0.0, "seed": 0, "max_tokens": 64, "logprobs": 5, "stream": False, } decode_response = requests.post( "http://127.0.0.1:8200/v1/completions", json=decode_payload, headers={"X-Request-Id": request_id}, timeout=180, ) print("decode status:", decode_response.status_code) print("decode body:", decode_response.text) ``` Observed result: ```text decode status: 200 ``` Repeat this process three times with three independently generated markers and request IDs. ## Monolithic control After recording the P/D outputs, stop both the prefill and decode servers. Start a monolithic server without LMCache or any other KV connector: ```bash CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=0 \ python -m vllm.entrypoints.openai.api_server \ --model Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B \ --served-model-name veritas-model \ --host 127.0.0.1 \ --port 8300 \ --dtype bfloat16 \ --max-model-len 2048 \ --max-num-seqs 8 \ --gpu-memory-utilization 0.65 \ --no-enable-prefix-caching \ --disable-log-stats \ --enforce-eager ``` Replay each previously recorded prompt byte-for-byte: ```python monolithic_payload = { "model": "veritas-model", "prompt": prompt, "temperature": 0.0, "seed": 0, "max_tokens": 64, "logprobs": 5, "stream": False, } monolithic_response = requests.post( "http://127.0.0.1:8300/v1/completions", json=monolithic_payload, headers={"X-Request-Id": f"mono-{request_id}"}, timeout=180, ) print("monolithic status:", monolithic_response.status_code) print("monolithic body:", monolithic_response.text) ``` Observed result: ```text monolithic status: 200 ``` ## Comparison oracle For every prompt, compare the P/D result with the monolithic result using: 1. Generated token strings. 2. Generated text. 3. Selected-token log probabilities. 4. Top-5 token overlap at each generated position. The equivalence requirements are: ```text Generated tokens must be identical. Generated text must be identical. Maximum selected-token logprob absolute difference must be <= 0.25. Minimum top-5 overlap across generated positions must be >= 0.80. ``` The following inputs are identical between the P/D decode and monolithic control: ```text Prompt bytes Model Model dtype Execution mode Temperature Seed Maximum generated tokens Requested logprob count Prefix-caching setting ``` ## LMCache transfer evidence In a representative vLLM 0.26.0 run, the LMCache decode receiver logged: ```text Reqid: cmpl-veritas-pd-0-... Total tokens 895 Inference Engine computed tokens: 0 LMCache hit tokens: 895 need to load: 894 ``` ```text Reqid: cmpl-veritas-pd-1-... Total tokens 897 Inference Engine computed tokens: 0 LMCache hit tokens: 897 need to load: 896 ``` ```text Reqid: cmpl-veritas-pd-2-... Total tokens 897 Inference Engine computed tokens: 0 LMCache hit tokens: 897 need to load: 896 ``` In the vLLM 0.27.1 confirmation run, the receiver similarly logged: ```text Reqid: cmpl-veritas-pd-0-... Total tokens 897 Inference Engine computed tokens: 0 LMCache hit tokens: 897 need to load: 896 ``` ```text Reqid: cmpl-veritas-pd-1-... Total tokens 897 Inference Engine computed tokens: 0 LMCache hit tokens: 897 need to load: 896 ``` ```text Reqid: cmpl-veritas-pd-2-... Total tokens 895 Inference Engine computed tokens: 0 LMCache hit tokens: 895 need to load: 894 ``` The connector evidence collected from the server logs was: ```json { "lmcache_initialized": true, "pd_enabled": true, "nixl_channel": true, "cache_retrieval": true, "healthy_engine": true } ``` ## Representative output mismatch For one vLLM 0.26.0 repetition, the LMCache P/D output began with: ```text alpha beta gamma delta epsilon zeta eta theta alpha beta gamma delta epsilon zeta eta theta alpha beta gamma delta epsilon zeta eta theta ``` Its first generated tokens were: ```json [ " alpha", " beta", " gamma", " delta", " epsilon", " z", "eta", " eta", " theta", " alpha", " beta", " gamma" ] ``` For the identical prompt, the monolithic output began with: ```text The problem is to summarize the operational sequence in exactly three short bullets. ``` Its first generated tokens were: ```json [ " ", "The", " problem", " is", " to", " summarize", " the", " operational", " sequence", " in", " exactly", " three" ] ``` The P/D and monolithic generations therefore diverged at generated token 0. A second prompt produced the following P/D output: ```text alpha. alpha. alpha. alpha. alpha. alpha. alpha. alpha. alpha. alpha. alpha. alpha. alpha. alpha. alpha. alpha. ``` The monolithic server instead produced: ```text The first step is to identify the key elements of the system. The second step is to determine the appropriate tools and methods to achieve the goal. The third step is to implement the solution. ``` ## vLLM 0.26.0 results ### Independent run 1 ```text Prompt 0: tokens_equal: false text_equal: false maximum selected-token logprob difference: 3.4423 minimum top-5 overlap: 0.0 Prompt 1: tokens_equal: false text_equal: false maximum selected-token logprob difference: 3.6104 minimum top-5 overlap: 0.0 Prompt 2: tokens_equal: false text_equal: false maximum selected-token logprob difference: 3.3309 minimum top-5 overlap: 0.0 ``` ### Independent run 2 ```text Prompt 0: tokens_equal: false text_equal: false maximum selected-token logprob difference: 3.3705 minimum top-5 overlap: 0.0 Prompt 1: tokens_equal: false text_equal: false maximum selected-token logprob difference: 3.4516 minimum top-5 overlap: 0.0 Prompt 2: tokens_equal: false text_equal: false maximum selected-token logprob difference: 3.3782 minimum top-5 overlap: 0.0 ``` Result: ```text 6/6 LMCache P/D comparisons failed. All six comparisons diverged at generated token 0. ``` ## vLLM 0.27.1 results ```text Prompt 0: tokens_equal: false text_equal: false maximum selected-token logprob difference: 3.6067 minimum top-5 overlap: 0.0 Prompt 1: tokens_equal: false text_equal: false maximum selected-token logprob difference: 3.6052 minimum top-5 overlap: 0.0 Prompt 2: tokens_equal: false text_equal: false maximum selected-token logprob difference: 2.5831 minimum top-5 overlap: 0.0 ``` Result: ```text 3/3 LMCache P/D comparisons failed. All three comparisons diverged at generated token 0. ``` ## Native NIXL control The identical three prompts and monolithic-equivalence oracle were run using the native vLLM NIXL connector. ```text Prompt 0: tokens_equal: true text_equal: true maximum selected-token logprob difference: 0.0479 minimum top-5 overlap: 0.8 Prompt 1: tokens_equal: true text_equal: true maximum selected-token logprob difference: 0.0893 minimum top-5 overlap: 0.8 Prompt 2: tokens_equal: true text_equal: true maximum selected-token logprob difference: 0.0621 minimum top-5 overlap: 0.8 ``` Native NIXL verdict: ```text pass ``` ## Mooncake control The identical three prompts and monolithic-equivalence oracle were also run using the Mooncake connector. ```text Prompt 0: tokens_equal: true text_equal: true maximum selected-token logprob difference: 0.0942 minimum top-5 overlap: 0.8 Prompt 1: tokens_equal: true text_equal: true maximum selected-token logprob difference: 0.1162 minimum top-5 overlap: 0.8 Prompt 2: tokens_equal: true text_equal: true maximum selected-token logprob difference: 0.0640 minimum top-5 overlap: 0.8 ``` Mooncake verdict: ```text pass ``` These controls use the same: ```text Model Prompt generation Prompt lengths GPU type BF16 dtype Temperature Seed Maximum generated token count Logprob count Monolithic-equivalence oracle ``` ## Reproducibility summary | Runtime | Connector | Comparisons | Result | |---|---|---:|---| | vLLM 0.26.0 / LMCache 0.5.3-g140819c9, run 1 | LMCache | 3 | 3 mismatches | | vLLM 0.26.0 / LMCache 0.5.3-g140819c9, run 2 | LMCache | 3 | 3 mismatches | | vLLM 0.27.1 / LMCache 0.5.3-g140819c9 | LMCache | 3 | 3 mismatches | | vLLM 0.26.0 | Native NIXL | 3 | 3 equivalent | | vLLM 0.26.0 | Mooncake | 3 | 3 equivalent | Overall LMCache result: ```text 9/9 P/D versus monolithic comparisons mismatched. ``` ## Expected behavior When the LMCache receiver reports that the complete prompt KV cache was retrieved, decoding should be semantically equivalent to running the same prompt on a monolithic server with the same model and sampling configuration. In particular: - The first generated token should match. - The complete generated token sequence should match. - The generated text should match. - Token log probabilities should remain within normal BF16 numerical tolerance. - Top-k distributions should retain substantial overlap. ## Actual behavior The LMCache receiver reports a complete KV-cache hit and returns HTTP 200, but: - The first generated token differs from the monolithic result. - The complete 64-token output differs. - Generated text differs. - Minimum top-5 overlap reaches 0.0. - Maximum selected-token logprob differences reach approximately 2.58–3.61. - Output frequently begins with tokens taken from inside the repeated prompt body. - Both servers remain healthy. - No explicit runtime error is returned to the client. ## Classification This appears to be a remote KV restoration correctness failure rather than a transfer availability failure. The evidence shows that: - LMCache initializes successfully. - P/D mode is enabled. - The NIXL/UCX transfer path is active. - The receiver reports complete cache hits. - The inference engine reports zero computed prompt tokens. - Prefill and decode requests both return HTTP 200. - Both engines remain healthy. - The restored KV state does not preserve the expected next-token semantics. ## Reproduce * The full reproduction script can be seen here [repro_lmcache_pd.py](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/31142926/repro_lmcache_pd.py). * Run it with 2 separate GPUs. `.../miniconda3/envs/vllm_0260/bin/python repro_lmcache_pd.py --prefill-gpu 0 --decode-gpu 1 --out-dir artifacts` ### Before submitting a new issue... - [x] Make sure you already searched for relevant issues, and asked the chatbot living at the bottom right corner of the [documentation page](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/), which can answer lots of frequently asked questions.

signal.title: [Kernel] Skip padding rows in SiTU activation for DeepEP v2 decode
signal.text: ## Purpose Skip padding rows in the SiTU (SituGLU) activation kernel during DeepEP v2 decode. With DeepEP v2, the receive buffer is worst-case allocated (`num_max_tokens_per_rank * world_size`), but during decode only a fraction of rows hold valid tokens. The `situ_and_mul` kernel was launching one block per row over the whole buffer, so for typical decode batches most of that compute was spent on padding (roughly 87% wasted for the batch sizes we measured on Kimi-K3). This threads the device-side `psum_recv_per_rank` count from DeepEP v2 through `ExpertTokensMetadata` -> `HummingIndexedExperts` -> `apply_moe_activation` -> the `situ_and_mul` CUDA op, and adds an early-exit so blocks past the valid row count return immediately. The count is read through a device pointer inside the kernel, so it stays CUDA-graph safe (no host sync, value resolved at launch time). ## Changes - `situ_and_mul` gains an optional `valid_rows` tensor argument (`Tensor? valid_rows=None`); the kernel returns early when `row >= *valid_rows_ptr`. `valid_rows=None` preserves the previous full-buffer behavior for every other caller. - `ExpertTokensMetadata` carries an optional `psum_recv_per_rank`; DeepEP v2 populates it only in cudagraph (decode) mode. - `HummingIndexedExperts.apply()` derives `valid_rows = psum_recv_per_rank[-1] * topk` and forwards it to the activation. Non-Humming activations and the prefill path are unaffected: `psum_recv_per_rank` stays `None`, so `valid_rows` is `None`. ## Test Plan Correctness is covered by the existing GSM8K humming configs (the padded rows contain no valid tokens, so masking them cannot change output). The win is a decode-time reduction in blocks launched by the SiTU kernel; benchmark numbers on H200 to follow. 🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)

signal.title: [Attention] Enable adaptive verification for FLASHINFER_MLA_SPARSE_DSV4
signal.text: ## Purpose Follow-up to #47808. The FlashInfer sparse MLA decode kernel (`flashinfer_trtllm_batch_decode_sparse_mla_dsv4`) supports variable query lengths via `cum_seq_lens_q` / `max_q_len`, but the backend's metadata builders reported `AttentionCGSupport.UNIFORM_BATCH` instead of `ALWAYS`. Adds thin metadata builder subclasses (MLA + SWA) that declare `AttentionCGSupport.ALWAYS`, mirroring the pattern established by the FlashMLA backend in `flashmla.py`, and wires them into `DeepseekV4FlashInferMLASparseBackend` and both attention classes. ## Test Plan - Existing `tests/v1/attention/test_sparse_mla_backends.py` validates FlashInfer sparse MLA kernel correctness (no behavioural change to the forward path). - End-to-end: run DeepSeek-V4 with `enable_adaptive_verification: true` on FLASHINFER_MLA_SPARSE_DSV4 — the runtime assertion that previously raised the error now passes. --- <details> <summary> Essential Elements of an Effective PR Description Checklist </summary> - [ ] The purpose of the PR, such as "Fix some issue (link existing issues this PR will resolve)". - [ ] The test plan, such as providing test command. - [ ] The test results, such as pasting the results comparison before and after, or e2e results - [ ] (Optional) The necessary documentation update, such as updating `supported_models.md` and `examples` for a new model. </details>

signal.title: [RFC]: Pluggable KV Cache Data Types
signal.text: ### Motivation. The `--kv-cache-dtype` CLI parameter currently accepts only the values listed in the `CacheDType` literal: ```python CacheDType = Literal[ "auto", "float16", "bfloat16", "fp8", "fp8_e4m3", "fp8_e5m2", "fp8_inc", "fp8_ds_mla", "turboquant_k8v4", "turboquant_4bit_nc", "turboquant_k3v4_nc", "turboquant_3bit_nc", "int4_per_token_head", "int8_per_token_head", "fp8_per_token_head", "nvfp4", ] ``` These are hard-coded. Adding a new KV cache dtype requires modifying vLLM core in at least four places: 1. **`CacheDType` literal** — add the string 2. **`STR_DTYPE_TO_TORCH_DTYPE`** — map it to a `torch.dtype` 3. **`KVQuantMode`** — map it to specified quant mode 4. **`is_quantized_kv_cache()`** — teach it the new dtype's properties This makes it impossible for: - **Hardware backends** — to ship their own KV cache quantization format without editing vLLM (e.g., a new device-specific int8 variant) - **Third-party quantization libraries** — to integrate directly The quantization methods system (`--quantization`) already solved this exact problem with `register_quantization_config`. KV cache dtype should follow the same pattern. ### Proposed Change. > **Status:** Implemented in [PR #52670](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/52670). > The design below is the finalized contract. The design follows the pattern established by `register_quantization_config` in `vllm/model_executor/layers/quantization/__init__.py`. ### 1. Define a KV Cache Dtype Plugin Interface ```python class KVCacheDTypeHandler(Protocol): """Contract for a registered `--kv-cache-dtype` value. A backend implements this interface to answer the questions vLLM currently answers with closed tables (STR_DTYPE_TO_TORCH_DTYPE / get_kv_quant_mode / is_quantized_kv_cache). A single handler may be device-aware (e.g., resolving different torch dtypes per Ascend generation). """ # Public name, e.g. "int8". Must match the registration key. name: str def torch_dtype(self, *args, **kwargs) -> torch.dtype: """Storage dtype for KV cache tensors. Called **once at registration time** and injected into the shared STR_DTYPE_TO_TORCH_DTYPE dict, so all existing direct dictionary access sites need no changes. May query the current platform.""" ... def is_quantized(self) -> bool: """True if the cache is quantized (non-native dtype). Replaces the ad-hoc string matching in is_quantized_kv_cache.""" ... def quant_mode(self) -> KVQuantMode: """Maps to the upstream KVQuantMode enum used by generic kernels, or returns KVQuantMode.NONE / a new BACKEND sentinel when the backend fully self-manages dispatch.""" ... ``` #### 1.2 `KVQuantMode.BACKEND` sentinel `quant_mode()` may return the new `KVQuantMode.BACKEND` when the backend fully self-manages kernel dispatch. Its semantics: - Reads as **quantized** (distinct from `KVQuantMode.NONE`, which means non-quantized). - Matches **no generic kernel mode**: `is_per_token_head is False`, `is_nvfp4 is False`, and it is not equal to `NONE`. - Signals to the attention selector / dispatch layer that the backend owns kernel selection — generic per-token-head / fp8 kernel paths must not be selected for it. ### 2. Registration API (inspired by `register_quantization_config`) ``` # 1. Upstream-known defaults (the closed Literal stays for docs / IDE / type-checking) # 2. Mutable mirror — custom entries are appended here KV_CACHE_DTYPES: list[str] = list(get_args(CacheDType)) # 3. Handler registry: name -> KVCacheDTypeHandler instance (eager) _KV_CACHE_DTYPE_HANDLERS: dict[str, KVCacheDTypeHandler] = {} def register_kv_cache_dtype(name: str): """Register a custom `--kv-cache-dtype` value (decorator, eager). @register_kv_cache_dtype("int8") class Int8Handler: def torch_dtype(self): ... def is_quantized(self): ... def quant_mode(self): ... During decoration the handler will: (a) append to the mutable KV_CACHE_DTYPES list (driving Pydantic + CLI validation); (b) resolve torch_dtype() once and **inject into STR_DTYPE_TO_TORCH_DTYPE**, so all existing `dict[name]` / `name in dict` sites need zero changes; (c) be stored for later quant_mode()/is_quantized() queries. """ def _decorate(cls): if name in KV_CACHE_DTYPES: # Override: warn but allow (replicates register_quantization_config) ... else: KV_CACHE_DTYPES.append(name) inst = cls() # Critical step: mutate shared dtype dict in-place — downstream zero changes STR_DTYPE_TO_TORCH_DTYPE[name] = inst.torch_dtype() _KV_CACHE_DTYPE_HANDLERS[name] = inst return cls return _decorate def get_kv_cache_dtype_handler(name: str) -> KVCacheDTypeHandler | None: """Return the handler for `name`; returns None for upstream dtypes that have no handler (the dtype table already covers these).""" return _KV_CACHE_DTYPE_HANDLERS.get(name) def is_known_kv_cache_dtype(name: str) -> bool: return name in KV_CACHE_DTYPES ``` The decorator **only touches platform-independent state** — `KV_CACHE_DTYPES`, `STR_DTYPE_TO_TORCH_DTYPE`, and the handler map. It deliberately does **not** read `current_platform`: an OOT backend registers from its `Platform.__init__`, where accessing `current_platform` would re-enter `__getattr__("current_platform")` while `_current_platform` is still `None` (assignment happens after instantiation returns), recursing. Keeping the decorator platform-agnostic mirrors `register_quantization_config`, whose decorator likewise stays off `current_platform`. Platform activation — and with it any OOT backend's `@register_kv_cache_dtype` decorators — is triggered separately by the `CacheConfig` validator (§4, §6), at a point where the platform is fully resolved. ### 3. Integrate Into Core Dispatch Points #### 3.1 quant-mode dispatch ```python def get_kv_quant_mode(kv_cache_dtype: str) -> KVQuantMode: handler = get_kv_cache_dtype_handler(kv_cache_dtype) if handler is not None: return handler.quant_mode() ... # existing branches ``` #### 3.2 `is_quantized_kv_cache` The duplicate `is_quantized_kv_cache` helpers (`vllm/v1/kv_cache_interface.py:77-83` **and** `vllm/utils/torch_utils.py:75-85` — currently two parallel implementations) should be merged into a single registry-aware implementation. `kv_cache_uses_per_token_head_scales()` follows the same handler-first / string-fallback pattern. Callers are repointed to `vllm.utils.torch_utils`. ### 4. Relax `CacheDType` Validation ``` # `vllm/config/cache.py:76` # Before cache_dtype: CacheDType = "auto" # After — accept arbitrary strings, validate against registry cache_dtype: CacheDType | str = "auto" ``` This replicates `quantization: QuantizationMethods | str | None` (`vllm/config/model.py:203`). Pydantic no longer rejects custom strings. The `CacheConfig.cache_dtype` validator: 1. touches `current_platform` to trigger platform activation, which lets out-of-tree backends register their dtypes (via `@register_kv_cache_dtype` in their `Platform.__init__`) into `KV_CACHE_DTYPES` / `STR_DTYPE_TO_TORCH_DTYPE` **before** membership is checked; 2. then `is_known_kv_cache_dtype(dtype)` rejects unknown names with `ValueError`. There is no per-platform whitelist. A backend that needs to reject a dtype on its device raises from its own `Platform.__init__` (or a higher-level config check), not from the `CacheConfig` validator. The single global registry is the sole gate. ### Feedback Period. _No response_ ### CC List. _No response_ ### Any Other Things. _No response_ ### Before submitting a new issue... - [x] Make sure you already searched for relevant issues, and asked the chatbot living at the bottom right corner of the [documentation page](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/), which can answer lots of frequently asked questions.

### 🐛 Describe the bug ## Summary With `OffloadingConnector` + `CPUOffloadingSpec`, KV blocks are written to host memory correctly but are **never read back** while speculative decoding is enabled. Disabling `--speculative-config` — changing nothing else — makes the same workload serve from the CPU tier immediately. The CPU tier appears not to *retain* entries: `kv_offload_cpu_cache_usage_perc` rises while a request is in flight and returns to `0.0` as soon as the engine goes idle, never accumulating across requests. Lookups run ( `kv_offload_lookup_sync_delay_seconds_count` increments) and always miss, and the `CPU_to_GPU` transfer metric is absent entirely rather than merely small. ## Environment - Intel Arc Pro B70 32 GB, single card, `device_config=xpu`, TP=1 - vLLM built from source, `main` @ `3756bf1e2ba0909500fbe77e03fe02eafb7f7080` - vllm-xpu-kernels @ `4509e9f9791299e24622cb1d4ff63b61cd03925a` - Model: `Vishva007/Qwen3.8-27B-W4A16-AutoRound-GPTQ` — `Qwen3_5ForConditionalGeneration`, dense, 64 layers with hybrid linear_attn / full_attention, 24 Q / 4 KV heads, head_dim 256, `mtp_num_hidden_layers: 1` - `--dtype float16 --kv-cache-dtype fp8 --enable-prefix-caching --mamba-cache-mode align --max-model-len 179200 --max-num-seqs 8 --max-num-batched-tokens 16384 --enable-chunked-prefill` - `--kv-transfer-config '{"kv_connector":"OffloadingConnector","kv_role":"kv_both","kv_connector_extra_config":{"spec_name":"CPUOffloadingSpec","cpu_bytes_to_use":17179869184}}'` Startup logs this, as expected: ``` Creating offloading spec with name: CPUOffloadingSpec KV offloading: EAGLE/MTP draft attention groups [0, 1, 2, 3] detected. The trailing chunk of these groups will be excluded from offloading due to volatility. ``` Note the fallback at `offloading/scheduler.py:218-219` marks **every** group as an eagle group, because no group self-identifies via `is_eagle_group` on this model (MTP shares the target's weights/KV). ## Reproduction `max_tokens=1` on every request, so wall time is essentially prefill. 1. send prompt A (~29.8K tokens) — cold 2. send A again — GPU prefix-cache hit 3. send 7 distinct ~35K-token prompts — flushes the 179,200-token GPU cache 4. send A again — GPU-evicted; should be served from the CPU tier Host pool is sized so the flush cannot evict A from CPU: 8 prompts × ~1.4 GB ≈ 11.5 GB against a 16 GiB pool, and the run's own `kv_offload_total_bytes_total{GPU_to_CPU}` confirms 11.69 GB stored. ## Results | step | `--speculative-config` MTP **on** | MTP **off** | |---|---|---| | 1. cold | 17.84 s | 16.59 s | | 2. GPU-cached | 1.92 s | 0.74 s | | 4. post-evict | **16.78 s** (recomputed) | **1.61 s** (served) | MTP off, the arithmetic closes exactly: ``` step 4 (CPU fetch) 1.61 s step 2 (GPU cache) 0.74 s ------- difference 0.87 s ≈ kv_offload_load_time_total = 0.851 s ``` ### Metrics, MTP on ``` kv_offload_total_bytes_total{transfer_type="GPU_to_CPU"} = 1.1685986304e+10 (11.69 GB, 24 transfers) kv_offload_total_bytes_total{transfer_type="CPU_to_GPU"} = (absent) kv_offload_store_bytes_total = 1.1685986304e+10 kv_offload_lookup_sync_delay_seconds_count = 10 ``` Per-window `kv_offload_cpu_cache_usage_perc` against `Running`: ``` Running: 0 usage 0.0 Running: 1 usage 0.0844 <- 8.44% of 16 GiB = ~1.45 GB = exactly one prompt Running: 0 usage 0.0 Running: 1 usage 0.0844 Running: 0 usage 0.0 ``` It never exceeded 0.088 across the whole run, so LRU eviction was never in play. ### Metrics, MTP off (only change) ``` kv_offload_total_bytes_total{transfer_type="CPU_to_GPU"} = 1.097662464e+09 (1.10 GB) kv_offload_load_bytes_total = 1.097662464e+09 kv_offload_load_time_total = 0.851 s kv_offload_load_size_count = 1 ``` `kv_cache_size_tokens` also rises 179,200 → 215,647 with the draft model gone, but that only changes how much is evicted, not whether reads happen at all. ## What I ruled out - **Undersized pool.** Usage peaks at one prompt and returns to zero; the pool never fills. Raising 8 GiB → 16 GiB changed nothing. - **A lookup-side off-by-one.** `is_eagle_unverified` widens the query by one chunk only for sliding-window groups (`scheduler.py:695-700`) but applies `num_hit_chunks -= 1` unconditionally (`:733`). This model has no sliding window (`sliding_window="None"`), so the decrement is uncompensated. I patched `:696` to widen for all eagle groups and it made **no difference** — and on reflection an ~18-chunk prompt losing one chunk should produce a partial hit, not a total miss. So this asymmetry looks wrong but is not the cause. - **`offload_prompt_only`.** Already defaults to `True` (`v1/kv_offload/base.py:597`), so the volatile decode tail should already be excluded. The evidence points at the **store/retention** path rather than lookup: entries are written and counted, then not committed for future lookup, so lookups search an empty index. Other `is_eagle_group` sites I have not traced are `scheduler.py:359` (store-side chunk decrement while decoding) and the `is_store_reachable_swa_chunk` gate. ## Ask Is `OffloadingConnector` expected to work with EAGLE/MTP speculative decoding at all, particularly on hybrid Mamba/GDN + attention models? If the volatility handling is meant to exclude only the trailing chunk, something is dropping the whole entry instead. Happy to run instrumented builds — the reproduction is deterministic and takes about three minutes. ### Before submitting a new issue... - [x] Make sure you already searched for relevant issues, and asked the chatbot living at the bottom right corner of the [documentation page](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/), which can answer lots of frequently asked questions.

signal.title: [Bugfix][MiniMax-M3] Keep FP8 query allocation stable across CUDA graph replay
signal.text: ## Purpose MiniMax-M3 allocates its FP8 query buffer outside an eager CUDA-graph break, but the current allocation condition depends on request metadata that is re-evaluated inside the eager attention segment. A graph captured without a CUTLASS MSA plan can later replay with a valid plan, causing the eager CUTLASS path to receive `query_fp8=None` and fail at `assert query_fp8 is not None`. Allocate `query_fp8` whenever the configured implementation supports CUTLASS decode, which is static across capture and replay. Keep the per-request CUTLASS-versus-Triton decision inside the eager segment. CUTLASS-capable configurations may therefore produce the FP8 query for request shapes that fall back to Triton; this keeps the graph output stable without changing dynamic backend selection. This does not duplicate an existing contribution. Before opening this PR, open vLLM issues and PRs were searched for `query_fp8 MiniMax`, `use_cutlass_decode MiniMax`, and the CUDA-graph replay failure; no matching fix was found. The search was repeated while rebasing onto current `main`, and no overlapping open PR was found. This is an AI-assisted contribution. OpenAI Codex provided non-trivial assistance with the implementation, test, and rebase. The human submitter reviewed the changed lines and validation evidence before marking the PR ready. ## Test Plan - Exercise the actual MiniMax FP8 query allocation under a real `BreakableCUDAGraphCapture` on SM100. - Capture with CUTLASS enabled but no per-request CUTLASS plan. - Add the plan before replay, then verify repeated eager replays receive a non-null FP8 query at one stable CUDA address. - Run the existing MiniMax-M3 CUTLASS sparse-decode test file on SM100: `.venv/bin/python -m pytest -v -s tests/kernels/attention/test_minimax_m3_msa_cutlass_sparse_decode.py`. - Run pre-commit and mypy on the changed files. ## Test Result Static validation passed again after rebasing onto current `main`: - Full pre-commit hook set on both changed files. - Python 3.10 and Python 3.12 mypy hooks on both changed files. - Python bytecode compilation and `git diff --check`. The new CUDA regression was not rerun on the non-CUDA host because it requires SM100. Separate deterministic SM100 validation of the same transition used real `torch.cuda.CUDAGraph` and `BreakableCUDAGraphCapture`: - The parent behavior reproduced `assert query_fp8 is not None` when capture used the Triton fallback and replay became CUTLASS-eligible. - The patched behavior completed 100 replays. - All 101 capture/replay pointer observations were non-null and used one stable CUDA address. - The focused deterministic harness passed all 5 checks. Model/serving evaluation: a full MiniMax-M3 concurrency-512 A/B serving run completed successfully for both control and patched configurations. Aggregate token throughput changed by -0.34%, indicating no material performance regression in that comparison. A second independent concurrency-512 control/patched pair also completed end to end; neither arm reproduced the intermittent assertion in that pair.

signal.title: [Bugfix][Gemma4] Align enable_thinking default with chat template
signal.text: ## Purpose Fixes #49955. While investigating the trailing `<turn|>` token reported in #49955, I found an `enable_thinking` default mismatch between the bundled Gemma4 tool chat template and `Gemma4Parser`: ```python # examples/tool_chat_template_gemma4.jinja enable_thinking | default(false) # Gemma4Parser chat_kwargs.get("enable_thinking", True) ``` When `enable_thinking` is omitted, the chat template renders the prompt with thinking disabled, while the parser behaves as though thinking is enabled. In the affected streaming path, this can leave the outer delegating parser and the inner Gemma4 parser engine in different states: ```text outer DelegatingParser: reasoning_ended = false route = reasoning parser inner Gemma4 parser engine: state = CONTENT ``` The model may then produce either an empty thought channel before the final content: ```text <|channel>thought <channel|> final content ``` or produce the final content directly without channel markers: ```text final content ``` I observed both forms during actual inference. In the empty-channel case, `<channel|>` produces a real `REASONING_END` event and happens to correct the outer parser state before the final content is emitted. In the direct-content case, no such event is produced, so the stream remains incorrectly routed through the reasoning adapter. This PR applies the narrow fix by aligning the parser default with the bundled chat template: ```python chat_kwargs.get("enable_thinking", False) ``` This makes the initial parser state consistent with the prompt that was actually rendered, so correct routing no longer depends on whether the model happens to generate an empty thought channel. Explicit `enable_thinking=true` behavior is unchanged. I also verified that applying #48748 to v0.26.0 prevents the literal `<turn|>` token from becoming user-visible in the original reproduction. However, #48748 is a generic special-token safety net: it drops the terminal token after the parser has already entered the inconsistent state. It masks the visible token leakage but does not resolve the underlying Gemma4 default and parser-state mismatch fixed here. This PR therefore does not add Gemma4-specific `<turn|>` suppression or modify generic `__DROP__` handling. <details> <summary>Broader alternative considered</summary> There is a broader possible fix: make the outer parser derive its initial reasoning state from the same open-channel check used by `adjust_initial_state_from_prompt()`. Relative to the current commit, the production-code change would be: ```diff diff --git a/vllm/parser/gemma4.py b/vllm/parser/gemma4.py --- a/vllm/parser/gemma4.py +++ b/vllm/parser/gemma4.py @@ def __init__( self, tokenizer, tools: list[Tool] | None = None, **kwargs, ) -> None: - chat_kwargs = kwargs.get("chat_template_kwargs", {}) or {} - # Keep the parser default aligned with tool_chat_template_gemma4.jinja. - self._thinking_enabled = chat_kwargs.get("enable_thinking", False) super().__init__( tokenizer, tools, **kwargs, ) @@ def is_reasoning_end(self, input_ids: list[int]) -> bool: - end_id = self._reasoning_end_token_id - start_id = self._reasoning_start_token_id - tool_call_id = self._tool_call_token_id - new_turn_id = self._new_turn_token_id - tool_response_id = self._tool_response_token_id - - if end_id is not None and not input_ids: - return self.parser_engine_config.initial_state != ParserState.REASONING - - for i in range(len(input_ids) - 1, -1, -1): - tid = input_ids[i] - if start_id is not None and tid == start_id: - return False - if tool_call_id is not None and tid == tool_call_id: - return True - if new_turn_id is not None and tid == new_turn_id: - return not self._thinking_enabled - if tool_response_id is not None and tid == tool_response_id: - return not self._thinking_enabled - if end_id is not None and tid == end_id: - return True - return True + # Keep outer routing aligned with adjust_initial_state_from_prompt(). + return not self._prompt_ends_in_open_reasoning(input_ids) ``` This alternative removes the outer/inner mismatch more generally, including when `enable_thinking=true`, by treating reasoning as open only when the prompt actually ends inside an unmatched `<|channel>` block. However, it also changes the meaning of `enable_thinking` in the initial routing decision. In particular, a thinking-enabled model turn may begin without an already-open channel and then generate `<|channel>` itself. I left this broader semantic change out of the submitted commit so that maintainers can decide whether configuration or the concrete prompt state should be the authoritative source for initial routing. </details> ## Test Plan Run the Gemma4 reasoning parser tests and the composed reasoning/tool streaming regression tests: ```bash python -m pytest -q \ tests/reasoning/test_gemma4_reasoning_parser.py \ tests/parser/engine/test_gemma4_turn_end.py ``` The regression coverage verifies that: * the parser default matches the bundled Gemma4 chat-template default when `enable_thinking` is omitted; * explicit `enable_thinking=true` behavior remains unchanged; * the outer delegating parser considers reasoning complete for a prompt rendered with thinking disabled; * the configured tool parser is dispatched; * normal streamed content is preserved; * the final `<turn|>` token is not returned as user-visible content. ## Test Result ```text ............................... [100%] 31 passed, 14 warnings in 23.44s ``` The warnings are unrelated existing PyTorch deprecation warnings for `torch.jit.script_method`. --- <details> <summary> Essential Elements of an Effective PR Description Checklist </summary> * [x] The purpose of the PR, such as "Fix some issue (link existing issues this PR will resolve)". * [x] The test plan, such as providing test command. * [x] The test results, such as pasting the results comparison before and after, or e2e results. * [x] No documentation update is required because this change aligns parser behavior with the existing bundled chat-template default. </details>

signal.title: [EPLB] Add contention-aware expert migration batching
signal.text: Partially addresses #31671. ## Summary Add opt-in `enable_migration_batching` for EPLB expert migration. The scheduler coalesces transfers for each directed rank pair and greedily groups flows so a rank communicates with at most one peer per batch. This reduces instantaneous NIC contention; the existing path is unchanged when batching is disabled. The scheduling idea is inspired by OmniInfer and adapted to vLLM's current sync/async EPLB paths and communicator interface, including NIXL's per-execution transfer context. This PR implements only the migration-instruction scheduling part of #31671, not topology-aware placement or a C++ scheduler. I searched open EPLB migration/scheduling PRs and found no duplicate implementation. AI assistance was used; the human submitter reviewed the changes and is responsible for the contribution. ## Tests ```bash .venv/bin/python -m pytest tests/distributed/test_eplb_migration_scheduler.py -q .venv/bin/pre-commit run --files \ vllm/config/parallel.py \ vllm/distributed/eplb/async_worker.py \ vllm/distributed/eplb/eplb_state.py \ vllm/distributed/eplb/migration_scheduler.py \ vllm/distributed/eplb/rebalance_execute.py \ tests/distributed/test_eplb_migration_scheduler.py ``` Result: `8 passed`; all selected pre-commit hooks passed. Serving used four Quadro RTX 6000 24 GB GPUs (one per node), `Qwen/Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct-2507`, TP=4, expert parallelism, 16 redundant experts, EPLB window/interval 50/100, concurrency 32, and prefix caching enabled. Each run used a fresh server. Sync used `torch_nccl`; async used `torch_gloo`. Both workloads tested sync/async with batching off/on. Commands used for the random workload: ```bash MODEL=Qwen/Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct-2507 vllm bench serve --backend vllm --model "$MODEL" --port 8000 \ --dataset-name random --random-prefix-len 300 \ --random-input-len 200 --random-output-len 100 \ --num-prompts 200 --max-concurrency 32 --seed 0 --temperature 0 \ --percentile-metrics ttft,tpot,e2el \ --metric-percentiles 50,90,95,99 --ignore-eos --disable-tqdm \ --save-result --result-dir "$RESULTS" --result-filename bench.json ``` Commands used for the ordered phased-English workload (256 prompts in eight 32-request CUDA/literature/mathematics/biomedical phases): ```bash MODEL=Qwen/Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct-2507 DATASET=/home/cc/benchmarks/eplb_upstream_phased_cache_on_20260818_r1/workload/eplb_phased_english_256.jsonl vllm bench serve --backend vllm --model "$MODEL" --port 8000 \ --dataset-name custom --dataset-path "$DATASET" --disable-shuffle \ --custom-output-len 100 --num-prompts 256 --max-concurrency 32 \ --seed 0 --temperature 0 --percentile-metrics ttft,tpot,e2el \ --metric-percentiles 50,90,95,99 --ignore-eos --disable-tqdm \ --save-result --result-dir "$RESULTS" --result-filename bench.json ``` All requests completed successfully with zero failures. NIC P99/peak is the head node's RX+TX rate sampled once per second during the benchmark; it is not reported by `vllm bench serve`. ## Results Random workload, prefix cache enabled: | Mode | Batch | Output tok/s | TTFT P50/P99 ms | TPOT P50/P99 ms | E2EL P99 ms | NIC P99/peak MB/s | | --- | --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | | sync | off | 20.22 | 40131.95 / 84048.68 | 1095.51 / 1478.92 | 186001.25 | 1852.22 / 1930.67 | | sync | on | 18.74 | 40319.07 / 85214.08 | 1209.60 / 1593.21 | 200128.55 | 1153.45 / 1210.99 | | async | off | 22.48 | 40601.85 / 81621.22 | 942.43 / 1347.07 | 162839.73 | 707.21 / 802.06 | | async | on | 22.85 | 40392.90 / 82462.42 | 929.03 / 1328.39 | 161767.77 | 649.08 / 701.98 | Phased-English workload, prefix cache enabled: | Mode | Batch | Output tok/s | TTFT P50/P99 ms | TPOT P50/P99 ms | E2EL P99 ms | NIC P99/peak MB/s | | --- | --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | | sync | off | 26.86 | 38503.30 / 67659.84 | 795.31 / 1129.39 | 134590.88 | 1829.08 / 1982.54 | | sync | on | 24.31 | 38687.32 / 80047.90 | 921.92 / 1259.57 | 156878.38 | 1161.40 / 1208.52 | | async | off | 30.29 | 38197.97 / 58619.07 | 693.25 / 1033.79 | 108864.96 | 799.65 / 914.92 | | async | on | 31.39 | 38335.24 / 59520.39 | 653.61 / 998.35 | 104369.71 | 705.32 / 770.31 | For async EPLB, batching improved output throughput by 1.6%/3.6% and reduced NIC P99 by 8.2%/11.8% on the random/phased workloads. signal.title: [Bug]: OpenAI `strict` flag on tool definitions is rendered into the model-visible chat template, changing tool-call behaviour
signal.text: ### Your current environment vLLM 0.24.0, `Qwen3.6-27B-FP8`, TP=2 (2× RTX 3090), served via `/v1/chat/completions`. Requests below go **directly to vLLM** (no gateway/proxy in the path). ### Describe the bug The request-level `strict` flag on a function definition (`tools[].function.strict`, part of the OpenAI protocol) is passed through to `apply_chat_template()` and therefore serialized verbatim into the `<tools>` block that the model sees. `strict` is a **server-side decoding directive** — vLLM uses it in `vllm/tool_parsers/structural_tag_registry.py::_any_tool_strict()` to decide whether to attach structural tags. It is not part of the JSON Schema the model needs. Leaking it into the prompt makes it model-visible, and the model reacts to it. #### 1. The field reaches the prompt (minimal, fully reproducible) Same request, only `strict` differing, via `/tokenize`: | `tools[0].function.strict` | prompt tokens | |---|---| | absent | 411 | | `false` | 416 | | `true` | 416 | `return_token_strs: true` shows it rendered inside the tools block: ``` ..."required": ["city"]}, "strict": false} </tools> ``` #### 2. It measurably degrades tool calling With a realistic agent payload (24 tools, ~3.8 KB system prompt, a task where calling a tool is optional), `strict: false` causes the model to emit a **malformed tool call as plain text in `content`** — an arguments-only object with no function name and no `<tool_call>` wrapper — instead of a real tool call. `finish_reason` is `stop`, `tool_calls` is empty. Identical request, only `strict` differing, 5 trials each, non-streaming: | `strict` | `tool_calls` | malformed call leaked into `content` | |---|---|---| | absent | **5/5** | 0/5 | | `false` | 0/5 | **4/5** | Example of what lands in `content`: ```json {"command": "cat << 'EOF' > \"$(dirname '$WORKSPACE')/essay.md\"\n...", "description": "Write essay to file"} ``` #### 3. It is semantic, not prompt-length noise Adding a **neutral filler string of the same token cost** to every tool description, with `strict` absent, does *not* reproduce it: | variant (24 tools, 5 trials) | `tool_calls` | |---|---| | `strict` absent | 4/4 | | `strict: false` | **0/4** | | `strict` absent + equal-length filler text | 4/4 | So it is the *meaning* of `"strict": false` in the tools block, not the extra tokens. #### 4. `strict: false` and absent take the identical server-side path `_any_tool_strict()` returns `False` for both, so with `tool_choice="auto"` both skip structural tags: ```python if tool_choice == "auto" and not _any_tool_strict(tools): return None ``` The only difference between the two requests is therefore what the **model** sees. ### Expected vs actual **Expected:** `strict` is consumed by the server to select the decoding strategy and does not appear in the rendered prompt. `strict: false` and an absent `strict` should be behaviourally identical, as the structural-tag code already treats them. **Actual:** `strict` is rendered into `<tools>`, and `strict: false` measurably degrades tool-call formatting relative to omitting the field. ### Where it happens `vllm/renderers/online_renderer.py`: ```python tool_dicts = [tool.model_dump() for tool in request.tools] ... tool_dicts=tool_dicts, # -> apply_chat_template(tools=...) ``` `model_dump()` is called with no `exclude`, so the whole function object — including `strict` — is handed to the chat template, which serializes it into `<tools>`. ### Suggested fix Exclude `strict` from the dicts passed to `apply_chat_template()`. vLLM has already consumed it (`_any_tool_strict()`) before this point, and a chat template has no way to know which fields are protocol-level rather than part of the function schema. ### Notes / limitations - The behavioural degradation (#2) needs a large, realistic tool set. It did **not** reproduce with 2, 3, or 6 tools, nor with the first 16 or 20 tools of the same set — in those cases both variants behave identically. The prompt-leak itself (#1) reproduces minimally with a single tool. - I have not tested >0.24.0. Between v0.24.0 and v0.27.1 I could find no merged PR touching this path (#40894 and #42292 are both already ancestors of v0.24.0). - This may be as much a chat-template question as a vLLM one, but vLLM controls what is passed to the template.

signal.title: [Bugfix][Quantization][XPU] Fix GPTQ MoE loading under moe_wna16
signal.text: > **Blocks [#52652](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/52652)** (tensor-descriptor path for `fused_moe_kernel_gptq_awq`) — this PR fixes the checkpoint-loading bugs that PR needs to reproduce its end-to-end results. This PR is independent and complete on its own. ## Summary Three independently-required fixes to load a real GPTQ MoE checkpoint through `--quantization moe_wna16`. Found running `Qwen/Qwen1.5-MoE-A2.7B-Chat-GPTQ-Int4`. | # | Fix | Failure without it | |---|---|---| | 1 | `moe_wna16` added to `XPUPlatform.supported_quantization` | `ValidationError: ... not supported in xpu` | | 2 | `packed_modules_mapping` propagated to the linear delegate in `moe_wna16.py` | fused layers built unquantized; `qweight`/`qzeros`/`scales` have nowhere to load | | 3 | XPU oracle guard + TRITON fallback in `int_wna16.py` | fix 1 alone lets a MoeWNA16 checkpoint reach XPU's native kernel, which contracts on a different weight layout and would mis-shape the tensor rather than reject it | **Fix 1** — nothing in `MoeWNA16Config` is CUDA-specific for GPTQ checkpoints; the allowlist simply never listed it. No-op on CUDA (`CudaPlatform` defines no allowlist at all). **Fix 2** — the delegate is rebuilt from the raw HF dict via `AutoGPTQConfig.from_config()`, which never sees `packed_modules_mapping` (attached to the *parent* config afterwards by the loader). Without it, `gate_up_proj`/`qkv_proj` match nothing in `modules_in_block_to_quantize`, so the layer registers only a plain `weight`. Now cached (`MoeWNA16Config.linear_quant_config`) so the loader's `maybe_update_config`/`apply_vllm_mapper` hooks — which `MoeWNA16Config` previously didn't forward at all — reach the same delegate instance `get_quant_method()` consults. Overlaps with [#35865](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/35865) (same gap), but that PR is stale (2026-05-23) and targets classes that no longer exist on current `main`. This is the minimal equivalent; happy to defer if #35865 is revived. **Fix 3** — the guard rejects the MoeWNA16 layout on XPU's native kernel explicitly (`_backend_incompatibility_reason`), naming `--moe-backend triton` as the fix. That alone left `--moe-backend auto` (the common case) dead-ending in a bare `NotImplementedError`, since TRITON was never an `auto` candidate on XPU. `_get_priority_backends()` now offers it as a fallback — no performance tradeoff, since TRITON is the only backend this layout can ever run on. ## Test plan 10 test functions / 15 parametrized cases in `tests/quantization/test_moe_wna16.py`, one per fix plus shared cases. Measured on real Intel B70: baseline (pristine `main`) **4 failed, 11 passed** → patched **15 passed**. Each fix also reverted individually on hardware, reproducing the failure in the table above. **End-to-end on both platforms, with `--moe-backend auto`** (not the explicit override — the fix under test is that `auto` must resolve correctly on its own). Both select and execute the same kernel (`Using TritonWNA16Experts` in the startup log, `fused_moe_kernel_gptq_awq` JIT-compiling at inference) and produce the identical generation for the same prompt — a strong signal for a weight-loading change: same weights, same places, same kernel, on both platforms. `ruff check` + `ruff format --check` clean. None of the three fixes execute during inference — fix 1 is a one-time allowlist check, fix 2's delegate build is now cached rather than rebuilt, fix 3 adds one candidate to a list consulted once per model construction — so no serving-path benchmark is included; there is no mechanism by which these changes could show up in one. --- AI assistance was used (Claude Code) for implementation and testing; every changed line was reviewed and all tests above were run personally on Intel B70 and NVIDIA B200 hardware.

signal.title: [Bug] Streaming input: zero-token continuation crashes EngineCore (Invalid request status: RUNNING) — client-triggerable via temperature>0 chat sessions
signal.text: ## Summary A streaming-input (resumable) session **kills the entire engine** (`EngineDeadError`) when a continuation turn produces **zero output tokens** — i.e. the model samples a stop token as the very first token of the turn. The scheduler then finds the resumed request still marked `RUNNING` in the waiting queue and raises, taking down `EngineCore` and every concurrent request on the server. This is a follow-up to #52471 (streaming-input depth costs); splitting the crash into its own issue because it is a distinct correctness/availability bug with a clean trigger. ## Severity The trigger is **ordinary chat traffic**: multi-turn sessions with temperature > 0 (the default for conversational serving; e.g. gemma-4's own `generation_config.json` ships `temperature: 1.0`). A zero-token stop-finish is a normal, per-turn sampling outcome, so a long enough conversation hits it with high probability — and one unlucky sample from one user crashes the shared engine for everyone. We observed **9 engine deaths across 5 fresh instances and 4 configurations**. ## Traceback (v0.25.1, deployed) ``` File ".../vllm/v1/engine/core.py", line 1304, in _process_engine_step outputs, model_executed = self.step_fn() File ".../vllm/v1/engine/core.py", line 547, in step_with_batch_queue scheduler_output = self.scheduler.schedule(self._should_throttle_prefills()) File ".../vllm/v1/core/sched/scheduler.py", line 981, in schedule raise RuntimeError(f"Invalid request status: {request.status}") RuntimeError: Invalid request status: RUNNING ``` The traceback is entirely within `EngineCore` → `Scheduler` — **no frontend frames**. It is reachable by any driver of streaming input (the native `AsyncLLM.generate()` async-generator interface, the `/v1/realtime` handler, or a custom router); our runs used a thin HTTP shim over `AsyncLLM.generate()`, but the shim is irrelevant to the crash. ## Trigger conditions (all three required) 1. **Streaming input / resumable session** — the request re-enters the update-and-requeue loop. One-shot requests are unaffected. 2. **A continuation turn generates zero output tokens** — the first sampled token is a stop/terminator token, so after the "discard last sampled token" step there is nothing left. Requires **temperature > 0** so a stop token can win the first draw; we hit it within 1–3 continuation turns at `temperature=0.7`. 3. **It is a continuation, not the first turn** — turn 1 of a fresh session never triggered it. ## Root-cause hypothesis `Scheduler._update_request_as_session()` keeps `_all_token_ids[num_prompt_tokens:num_computed_tokens]` and discards the final sampled token, on the assumption a finished turn produced ≥1 token. When the turn produced **zero** tokens (first sample was a stop token), this degenerates and the request is re-queued in a state the next `schedule()` pass rejects as invalid (`RUNNING` while waiting). This matches the "discard the last sampled output token" design described in the streaming-input blog, which implicitly assumes a token exists to discard. ## Reproduction Open a resumable streaming session and drive two turns of a chat model at `temperature=0.7`: - Turn 1: system preamble + a question + (in our case one image). Completes normally. - Turn 2: a follow-up question appended to the same session. Within a few such continuation turns, one returns `finish_reason=stop` with 0 tokens in ~15–20 ms, and the engine dies on the next schedule. **Negative control:** the identical turns at `temperature=0.0` complete normally, every time — isolating the zero-token sampling outcome as the cause (not request format; we also ruled out `max_num_batched_tokens`, `compile_ranges_endpoints`, and re-supplying the discarded stop token as text). A deterministic variant can be built by constructing a prompt where a stop token is the greedy first choice. Observed with a multimodal model; the mechanism is not image-specific and likely reproduces text-only. Happy to share our full runner script. ## Suggested fixes 1. Handle the zero-token completion in `_update_request_as_session()` (a turn that stops before generating leaves the session in a valid resumable state). 2. Make the scheduler's invalid-status check **fail the offending request**, not raise into `EngineCore` — a per-request error should not crash the whole engine (defense-in-depth regardless of root cause). ## Environment vLLM v0.25.1 (cu129), gemma-4-31b-it (multimodal), TP=4, streaming input via `AsyncLLM.generate()`.

signal.title: [3/N] Share HiSparse host cache across TP ranks
signal.text: ## Summary This PR optimizes #51324 with the following improvements: - Resolve shared/private Host pool mode in the KV cache planner. - Fall back to private pools when the Indexer block layout cannot be represented by the shared mmap layout. - Propagate the resolved mode and physical Host block stride through `KVCacheConfig`. - Roll back the shared Host region when GPU KV allocation or HiSparse worker initialization fails. - Check physical Host RAM only in the shared mmap creator process. - Fail joiners promptly when the creator fails and unlinks an incomplete mmap. - Add real multiprocess same-slot visibility coverage. - Clarify logical versus physical `host_pool_gib` capacity and startup logging. This is intentionally based on `feat/hisparse-metrics` so it remains the [3/N] change in the HiSparse stack. cc @MatthewBonanni

signal.title: [mooncake] support CUSTOM_MEM_POOL in vllm
signal.text: ### Purpose Add support for Mooncake custom memory pools (NVLINK / BAREX) when allocating KV cache in vLLM. This enables KV cache to use NVLink or BAR-exposed device memory instead of the default CUDA allocator, which is required by some MooncakeStoreConnector deployments for RDMA-based KV-cache transfer.When custom_mem_pool is configured in kv_connector_extra_config, MooncakeStoreConnector creates a torch.cuda.MemPool using the corresponding Mooncake allocator (NVLinkAllocator / BarexAllocator). When unset, the existing CuMem/default allocator behavior remains unchanged.Custom pools are incompatible with CuMem allocation and sleep mode. These conflicting configurations are rejected during connector initialization.In some scenarios, a specific allocator is required due to hardware limitations. ### Changes: -mooncake/store/worker.py: Validate custom_mem_pool, create and retain the Mooncake memory pool, detect CuMem/sleep-mode conflicts, and provide actionable errors for unsupported Mooncake versions. -mooncake/store/connector.py: Expose the custom memory-pool context to the GPU worker. -multi_connector.py: Forward a custom pool from child connectors and reject configurations where multiple children provide pools. -vllm/v1/worker/gpu_worker.py: Use a connector-provided pool during KV-cache allocation, while preserving the existing fallback behavior. -test_multi_connector.py: Add coverage for no pool, single-pool forwarding, and multiple-pool conflicts.

signal.title: [Bugfix] Add Kimi K3 MoE support to benchmark_moe.py
signal.text: ## Purpose `benchmarks/kernels/benchmark_moe.py` cannot tune the fused MoE Triton kernel for Kimi K3. `get_model_params()` does not recognize `KimiK3ForConditionalGeneration`, so it falls through to the Mixtral default branch and raises `AttributeError` (Kimi's config has no `num_local_experts`). Kimi K3 is multimodal and stores its MoE parameters in a nested `KimiLinearConfig` `text_config`, and it exposes the routing top-k as `num_experts_per_token` rather than the more common `num_experts_per_tok` used by the existing handlers. This adds a dedicated branch, following the same pattern as the Qwen3.5 handler added in #37068. It also covers the text-only `KimiLinearForCausalLM`, for which `get_text_config()` returns the config itself. ## Test Plan Parse the released Kimi K3 config and confirm the extracted MoE parameters: ```python from vllm.transformers_utils.config import get_config from benchmark_moe import get_model_params cfg = get_config("<path-to-Kimi-K3>", trust_remote_code=True) print(get_model_params(cfg)) ``` ## Test Result ``` architectures = ['KimiK3ForConditionalGeneration'] (text_config: KimiLinearConfig) get_model_params -> (E=896, topk=16, moe_intermediate_size=3072, hidden_size=7168) ``` The values match the model config. With `--tp-size 8 --enable-expert-parallel` this yields `E_local=112` and shard `N=6144`. Before this change the script raised `AttributeError` before tuning could start.

signal.title: [Feature]: KV Cache Eviction support ARC
signal.text: ### 🚀 The feature, motivation and pitch ## 1. The Problem ### 1.1 Pain Point: LRU Has No Memory of How Hot a Block Was vLLM's GPU KV cache (`BlockPool`) uses a **single-queue LRU** implemented in`FreeKVCacheBlockQueue`. When a request finishes, its blocks are appended to the tail of the free queue. When new blocks are needed, eviction drains from the head. This design has one fundamental blind spot: **once `ref_cnt` drops to zero, all blocks are equal candidates for eviction, regardless of how many times they were previously reused.** A system-prompt block touched by 10,000 requests and a one-time-use block are indistinguishable at eviction time. ### 1.2 Pain Point: Burst Requests Cause Scan Pollution In production, LLM serving commonly experiences **bursty traffic**: a wave of requests with unique prompts arrives simultaneously, each generating a large number of KV blocks that immediately become eviction candidates. These low-value blocks flood the tail of the free queue, pushing high-value cached prefix blocks toward the eviction head. This is the classic **scan pollution** problem, well-known in OS page-cache literature. Linux solved it decades ago with the Active/Inactive list design. vLLM has not yet applied equivalent protection to the GPU KV cache. ### 1.3 Why This Matters More Over Time | Deployment Trend | Effect on LRU Weakness | |---|---| | Longer system prompts (agents, RAG context) | More blocks per hot prefix → eviction loss per cache miss grows | | Higher concurrency | More simultaneous request completions → larger burst pollution events | | Disaggregated Prefill/Decode | Prefix blocks transferred from P → D must survive long enough to be reused; premature eviction nullifies the transfer cost | | Multi-tenant serving | Different tenants share the block pool; one tenant's burst can evict another's hot prefix | --- ## 2. Root Cause Analysis ### 2.1 Current Architecture BlockPool └── free_block_queue: FreeKVCacheBlockQueue # one doubly-linked list head (evict first) ←——————————————— tail (evict last) [ old cold blocks ] ... [ recently freed blocks ] The "reverse-order free" heuristic in `single_type_kv_cache_manager.py`: ```python # Free blocks in reverse order so that tail blocks are evicted first ordered_blocks = reversed(req_blocks) self.block_pool.free_blocks(ordered_blocks) ``` ### 2.2 Where the Logic Breaks Down Consider a 2,048-block GPU cache with a 64-block system prompt that has been reused by many requests: Timeline t=0 System prompt (64 blocks) used by 500 requests. ref_cnt > 0 → blocks NOT in free queue → safe. t=1 All 500 requests finish. ref_cnt drops to 0 → 64 blocks appended to queue TAIL. t=2 32 unique long-prompt requests arrive. Each uses 62 blocks → 1,984 blocks freed → appended to TAIL. Queue state after t=2: head [...stale blocks...][system-prompt 64 blocks][1,984 one-time blocks] tail ↑ evicted first ↑ evicted last t=3 Next batch needs 100 new blocks. Eviction drains from head → system-prompt blocks EVICTED before the 1,984 single-use blocks. The 64 most valuable blocks are lost before 1,984 worthless blocks. ### The Inconsistency: CPU Offload Already Has ARC vLLM already solved this problem for the CPU offload layer: ```python # vllm/v1/kv_offload/cpu/manager.py _CACHE_POLICIES = { "lru": LRUCachePolicy, "arc": ARCCachePolicy, # full T1/T2/B1/B2 ARC — already implemented } class CPUOffloadingManager: def __init__(self, num_blocks, cache_policy: Literal["lru", "arc"] = "lru"): self._policy = policy_cls(cache_capacity=num_blocks) ``` ARCCachePolicy (vllm/v1/kv_offload/cpu/policies/arc.py) provides: T1: recently accessed blocks (accessed once) T2: frequently accessed blocks (accessed multiple times) B1/B2: ghost lists for adaptive tuning The GPU BlockPool has no equivalent. This RFC proposes closing that gap. ## Quantified Impact ### Cache Miss Cost A prefix cache miss forces the engine to recompute tokens from scratch. For a model with hidden size 4096, 32 KV heads, 128 head dim, and block size 16: Cost to recompute one missed block ≈ 16 tokens × full prefill attention cost Typical TTFT (Time To First Token) regression from one evicted system-prompt block in a sequence of 2,048 tokens: Model Size | Block Recompute Time | Relative TTFT Increase -- | -- | -- 7B | ~3 ms | ~2–5% 13B | ~6 ms | ~4–8% 70B | ~25 ms | ~8–15% For a 64-block system prompt, multiply by 64. ### Hit Rate Simulation (Analytical Model) Assume: Pool: N = 2,048 blocks Hot prefix: H = 64 blocks, request arrival rate λ_h = 100 req/s Unique long prompts: L = 62 blocks/req, arrival rate λ_l = 10 req/s (burst) Under pure LRU, the hot prefix survives as long as: N - H = 1,984 unique-prompt blocks arrive between two consecutive hot-prefix-using requests. At λ_l = 10 req/s, a burst of 32 requests fills 1,984 blocks in ~3.2 seconds → hot prefix evicted in ~3.2 s of inactivity. Under Two-Queue: Hot prefix lives in the "hot" queue. Eviction drains the "cold" queue first (1,984 one-time blocks). Hot prefix is only touched after all 1,984 cold blocks are exhausted. Effective survival time: ∞ as long as cold blocks keep arriving. Expected hit-rate improvement in this workload: ~15–40% for system-prompt blocks, depending on burst intensity. ### Memory Overhead of the Fix Policy | Extra Data Structures | Memory Overhead -- | -- | -- LRU (current) | None | 0 Two-Queue (proposed) | 1 extra FreeKVCacheBlockQueue + set[int] | ~8 × N bytes for N=2048 → 16 KB ARC (future) | Ghost lists B1/B2, target_t1_size | ~48 × N bytes for N=2048 → 96 KB At 200,000 blocks (typical A100 80GB with Llama-3 70B), the Two-Queue overhead is ~1.6 MB — negligible against 80 GB GPU memory. ## Proposed Solution ### Design Principles - Zero behavior change by default. The existing LRU is wrapped, not replaced. Users who do not set - gpu_eviction_policy see identical behavior. - O(1) per operation. Scheduling is on the critical path; no linear scans. - Incremental. Two-Queue is a stepping stone toward full ARC, using the same abstraction. - Consistent with CPU layer. Mirror the pluggable CachePolicy design already used by CPUOffloadingManager. ### Architecture Overview ```text Before After ────────────────────── ────────────────────────────────────── BlockPool BlockPool └── free_block_queue └── _policy: GPUCachePolicy FreeKVCacheBlockQueue ├── LRUGPUCachePolicy (default) │ └── FreeKVCacheBlockQueue └── TwoQueueGPUCachePolicy ├── _cold: FreeKVCacheBlockQueue ├── _hot: FreeKVCacheBlockQueue └── _hot_set: set[int] ``` ### Alternatives _No response_ ### Additional context _No response_ ### Before submitting a new issue... - [x] Make sure you already searched for relevant issues, and asked the chatbot living at the bottom right corner of the [documentation page](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/), which can answer lots of frequently asked questions.

signal.title: [Build] Propagate vLLM version to Rust binaries
signal.text: ## Summary - derive a device-independent vLLM source version with setuptools-scm for Python-driven and standalone Rust builds - embed the same version in `vllm-rs`, `vllm-bench`, and the Rust frontend version endpoint - expose Git metadata to selective Docker Rust build stages while suppressing the artificial dirty state caused by omitted tracked files ## Affected outputs | Surface | Effect | | --- | --- | | `vllm-rs --version` | Reports the embedded vLLM source version. | | `vllm-bench --version` | Reports the embedded vLLM source version instead of the workspace crate version (`0.1.0`). | | Rust frontend `GET /version` | `rust_frontend_version` reports the embedded vLLM source version. The engine-reported `version` field keeps its existing behavior. | ## Affected build paths | Build path | Embedded Rust version | | --- | --- | | Nightly/release wheel builds from a Git checkout | The setuptools-scm source version. `VLLM_VERSION_OVERRIDE` is honored through `SETUPTOOLS_SCM_PRETEND_VERSION`. | | Docker builds using `docker/Dockerfile`, `.cpu`, `.rocm`, `.rocm_gfx1250`, or `.xpu` | The source version resolved from the mounted Git metadata. Selective-copy stages set `dirty=false` because omitted tracked files would otherwise make the partial worktree appear dirty. | | Local `bash build_rust.sh` | The setuptools-scm source version when Git metadata is available. | | Direct `cargo build` | `VLLM_RS_BUILD_VERSION` when explicitly supplied; otherwise the workspace crate version (`0.1.0`). | The embedded Rust version stays device-independent. Python distribution version handling remains unchanged, including platform suffixes such as CPU, CUDA, ROCm, TPU, and XPU variants. Repackaging an existing prebuilt Rust binary preserves the version embedded when that binary was built. ## Motivation Rust artifacts currently identify themselves using workspace crate metadata, which stays at `0.1.0` and does not identify the corresponding nightly or release vLLM source revision. This change resolves the source version before compiling Rust and passes it through `VLLM_RS_BUILD_VERSION`. `get_vllm_version()` runs first during Python packaging so `VLLM_VERSION_OVERRIDE`, propagated through `SETUPTOOLS_SCM_PRETEND_VERSION`, also applies to the Rust artifacts. ## Validation - `cargo nextest run -p vllm-build-info -p vllm-bench -p vllm-cmd -p vllm-server --no-fail-fast` (552 passed, 10 skipped) - injected version output: `vllm-bench 9.8.7` and `vllm-rs 9.8.7` - Cargo fallback output: `vllm-bench 0.1.0` - existing Docker build metadata tests (7 passed) - Ruff, Dockerfile parsing, shell syntax, and `git diff --check`

signal.title: [KV offload] Order CPU->GPU loads against the compute stream
signal.text: On models that zero freshly allocated KV blocks (any model with mamba layers, i.e. `needs_kv_cache_zeroing`), a CPU->GPU load in the offloading connector can be silently wiped. `SingleDirectionOffloadingHandler.transfer_async` waited on the compute stream only for GPU->CPU. Loads ran on their own stream with no ordering against the compute stream, which zeroes freshly allocated blocks. When the copy lands first, a pending zeroing of its destination blocks wipes it and the request attends over zeros for its whole cache-hit prefix. No crash, no error, just degraded output. Why the scheduler-side guard doesn't cover this: `_skip_zero_block_ids` only edits the zero list of the step being scheduled — it cannot retract a zeroing already shipped in an earlier step's `SchedulerOutput` for a since-reallocated block. Sync scheduling makes that safe implicitly: the engine blocks on each step's output, so shipped zeroing has provably executed before any later load submits. Async scheduling removes that wait, leaving the pair unordered across the two streams — safe by timing only, which nothing enforces. The skip set remains the only possible guard for writers that bypass CUDA streams (NIXL/RDMA); the stream wait is the only ordering against zeroing already dispatched. Verified on H100 that it is a real guard — same test, same image, with and without the one-line change: | | result | |---|---| | without the fix | fails, 4/5 trials, all 32 loaded blocks zeroed | | with the fix | passes, 5/5 trials |

signal.title: [Bugfix] Bound Gemma4 parser nesting depth
signal.text: ## Purpose Fixes #50927. Gemma4 tool-call argument parsing used a mutually recursive grammar without a depth bound. Deeply nested model output could therefore exhaust a worker thread's stack and terminate the process. This change rejects arguments nested deeper than 128 containers before entering the recursive parser. The pre-scan recognizes Gemma4's `<|"|>` string delimiters, so brackets inside string values do not count toward the nesting limit. ### Why 128 is safe The limit is inclusive: 128 container opens pass the guard, while the 129th is rejected. The reported crash required roughly 1,500 nested containers, so the parser is stopped more than an order of magnitude (about 11.7x) before the observed stack-exhaustion depth. The guard itself is a single linear scan with a constant-size counter, and it runs before recursive parsing. Duplicate-work checks found no open PR referencing #50927 and no open PR for the Gemma4 parser recursion issue. Model evaluation: not applicable. This is a parser-safety guard; valid tool calls within the supported nesting limit retain their existing behavior. AI assistance: Codex was used to implement and test this change. The human submitter reviewed every changed line. ## Test Plan ```bash cd rust cargo fmt --check cargo test -p vllm-parser gemma4_ ``` ## Test Result Passed: ```text running 33 tests test result: ok. 33 passed; 0 failed; 0 ignored; 0 measured; 387 filtered out ``` The focused suite covers the precise guard boundary (128 accepted; 129 rejected), rejection through both the argument parser and complete tool-call parser, and brackets inside Gemma4 string delimiters.
