signal.title: [RFC]: Complete Model Runner V2 pipeline parallelism: scheduling, speculative decoding, and PP-first DP/EP topology
signal.text: ### Motivation. > [!NOTE] > This RFC expands the original request-admission proposal into an end-to-end plan for Model Runner V2 (MRV2) pipeline-parallel feature composition. The original proposal remains Workstream A below, with its prototype in #50410. MRV2 pipeline parallelism (PP) already overlaps multiple batches to reduce pipeline bubbles (#42187). With asynchronous scheduling, it keeps `pp_size + 1` batch slots in flight, while a decode request becomes eligible again after a `pp_size`-step cadence. That foundation works for basic generation, but the surrounding features do not yet compose cleanly with PP: | Area | Current state | Gap addressed by this RFC | |---|---|---| | Request scheduling | Basic MRV2 PP works | A burst can fill the global request slots in one batch and leave later PP batches empty | | MTP speculative decoding | Work is in progress | Drafts produced and applied locally on the last rank must be published to non-last ranks and restored for the still-live rows of the stored step-`T` feedback slot | | EAGLE3, DFlash, and DSpark | Explicitly rejected with PP in MRV2 today | Auxiliary hidden states may be produced on earlier ranks but are consumed by the proposer on the last rank | | Index-sharing models | Rank-local buffers work when producer and consumer are colocated | A PP cut may fall between an index producer and a layer that reuses its top-k indices | | PP + DP/EP topology | Current deployments commonly place complete DP replicas contiguously | On multiple nodes this tends to keep PP local while DP/EP groups cross nodes; a PP-first placement should keep EP/TP inside a node and move PP traffic across nodes | The common theme is that PP is not only a partition of model layers. It also creates two state-transfer paths with different direction and lifetime: 1. **forward state**, sent from one PP rank to the next for the current microbatch; and 2. **deferred result state**, applied locally on the last rank and published to non-last ranks, which consume the stored `PPHandler` FIFO slot `pp_size` local feedback-ring steps later. Adding each new tensor with one-off communication code would make ordering, CUDA-graph capture, request-slot reuse, and multi-node topology assumptions increasingly fragile. This RFC therefore proposes both the missing feature support and a small declarative PP transport abstraction that can carry future optional state without redesigning the execution loop each time. #### Goals - Balance request admission across concurrent MRV2 PP batches. - Define correct MRV2 PP composition with MTP, EAGLE3, DFlash, and DSpark speculative decoding. - Carry auxiliary hidden states and cross-partition index-sharing state when a model partition requires them. - Define a PP-first multi-node placement in which each node hosts one complete PP stage's DP/EP domain, keeping EP/TP communication intra-node and PP communication inter-node. - Keep optional communication absent when a model or configuration does not need it. - Preserve static, graph-friendly buffer schemas and minimize extra collectives. #### Non-goals - Changing Model Runner V1. - Introducing a new speculative decoding algorithm. - Redesigning DP request routing, real/dummy execution cadence, or wave draining, or migrating live request/KV state between DP lanes. - Introducing a new pipeline schedule such as interleaved 1F1B. - Requiring every model to emit auxiliary hidden states or index buffers. - Enabling adaptive verification with PP in the first rollout; it needs a separate protocol for trimmed shapes, confidence/cost state, and rank agreement. - Supporting a PP-stage DP/EP footprint that cannot fit in a node-local topology domain in the first rollout. ### Proposed Change. Implement the RFC as four independently reviewable workstreams over one set of communication and correctness invariants. ```text current-microbatch forward plane scheduler -> PP rank 0 -> ... -> PP rank N (sample + propose) | IntermediateTensors | aux hidden states | shared indices | | +<---------- deferred result plane ----------+ sampled/count metadata and optional drafts (queued in the worker-side PPHandler feedback FIFO) PP-first multi-node placement: node 0 / PP stage 0: [DP0 ... DPN] <- EP/TP stays node-local | PP lanes | node 1 / PP stage 1: [DP0 ... DPN] <- EP/TP stays node-local ``` #### Workstream A: balance request admission across PP batches Within each scheduler/DP replica, the scheduler currently applies `max_num_seqs` as one global running-request limit and greedily fills a batch until an existing token, sequence, KV-cache, or model-specific constraint is reached. A burst of short, uniform requests can therefore consume all local request slots before the pipeline has formed multiple useful batches. For example: ```text pipeline_parallel_size = 2 max_num_seqs = 25 50 short requests arrive together ``` The current scheduler can produce `25, 0, 25, 0` scheduled requests over four steps. The prototype in #50410 instead caps the next batch at: ```python num_requests = min( max_num_running_reqs, get_num_unfinished_requests(), ) max_num_scheduled_reqs = ceil(num_requests / pp_size) ``` The prototype applies the cap to both requests already in `RUNNING` and admissions from `WAITING`, while all existing token, KV-cache, priority, preemption, structured-output, and model-specific constraints remain authoritative. In the example, the first two useful batches become approximately `13, 12` instead of `25, 0`. The divisor is `pp_size`, not `pp_size + 1`: the additional asynchronous queue entry covers result propagation and scheduler/worker overlap rather than an additional compute stage. Non-final chunked-prefill chunks remain eligible in adjacent steps because they do not depend on sampled-token feedback. This is intentionally a PP batch target, not a claim that request count always equals compute. Request count is a useful decode proxy; scheduled tokens are a better prefill proxy. The proposed MVP differs from the current prototype in one important respect: already-eligible `RUNNING` decode keeps its existing scheduling behavior, while the balance target is a soft cap on **new/resumed admission from `WAITING`**. The target may be exceeded when later phases have no runnable work, at low concurrency, at a KV/capacity boundary, or to prevent priority starvation. This preserves work conservation and avoids delaying active decode solely to make phase widths look uniform. Every DP replica computes this target locally. Evaluation should decide whether the final policy is request-count based, token based, or hybrid, and whether a persistent phase assignment is worth its complexity around completion, abort, preemption, resume, and priority changes. #### Workstream B: make PP state transport extensible Refactor PP state ownership into a small declarative module. `PPTransport`, `ForwardPayload`, and `DeferredResultPayload` below are conceptual names, not a required public API. One ownership module describes two independent schemas and communicators: **1. Forward payload: adjacent rank -> adjacent rank, current microbatch** - opaque model `IntermediateTensors` such as `hidden_states` and `residual`; - namespaced sidecars for auxiliary hidden states keyed by a global activation-boundary ID and configured slot; - a namespaced active top-k/index sidecar when the partition boundary crosses an index-reuse dependency. **2. Deferred result payload: last PP rank -> every non-last PP rank, delayed receiver slot** - sampled tokens; - sampled/rejected-token counts; - optional next-step draft tokens; - local queued request mappings and generation metadata that associate the received rows with still-live request slots (these do not need to be network fields). Each adjacent forward edge has its own field/liveness plan; the existing `PPHandler` sibling broadcast has one group-consistent feedback plan. They share descriptor and lifecycle machinery but not communicator, stream, cadence, or participant set. A conceptual field descriptor is: ```python @dataclass(frozen=True) class PPTensorSpec: name: str plane: Literal["forward", "deferred_result"] boundary_id: int | None slot: int | None dtype: torch.dtype trailing_shape: tuple[int, ...] tp_policy: Literal["replicated", "sharded", "direct"] carry: Literal[ "one_edge", "until_last", "until_consumed", "feedback_group" ] lifetime: Literal["forward_execution", "delayed_request_state"] ``` The exact fields can differ. The correctness MVP should run the declared plan over the existing tensor-dict path: - namespace and split opaque model tensors from optional sidecars; - keep each edge's field presence, key, dtype, slot ordering, carry policy, and TP policy deterministic after initialization; - export/import sidecars through model-specific adapters; - retain current tensor-dict metadata and allocation behavior where required for backend compatibility; - stream/event ownership and buffer reuse centralized in the transport module; - request generation/slot checks retained for delayed feedback, so an aborted or replaced request cannot consume stale state; - group-identical feedback row order, row count, dtype/shape, collective order, and whole-collective skip decisions; no branch on rank-local optional-field presence; - optional fields disabled add no bytes or collectives beyond the existing forward and sampled/count feedback paths. For forward sidecars, `N` means the execution row count after padding (`num_tokens_after_padding` / the batch execution descriptor), not only logical scheduled tokens. Buffers and wire shapes use `N`; adapters separately track which rows contain real tokens. For the initial models in this RFC, auxiliary hidden states are TP-replicated, and shared top-k is TP-replicated `[N, index_topk]` `torch.int32`. Existing model tensors such as sequence-parallel residual state retain their direct/sharded policy. Because the current tensor-dict path may automatically slice/all-gather based on tensor size, sidecar policy must be explicit rather than inferred from divisibility. Model-specific adapters should declare which sidecars a partition boundary needs, export locally produced fields, and import received fields into the correct persistent model buffer. The communication layer should not interpret EAGLE, DSpark, or model-specific index semantics. Namespaced wire keys such as `model/*`, `spec/aux_hidden_states`, and `model/shared_index_topk` can avoid collisions while keeping ordinary model tensors opaque. A later performance phase may compile a static wire schema, use persistent graph-address-stable receive buffers, and remove per-step CPU metadata. That requires explicit lower-level `GroupCoordinator`/backend protocol work and is not implied by adding the correctness wrapper. Compatible small fields should be packed when doing so removes latency-sensitive collectives, following the direction explored in draft #47686. Large auxiliary tensors should not be blindly packed with token metadata: grouping must respect direction, dtype, destination, lifetime, TP layout, and performance. The abstraction is unified at the ownership/schema layer, while the two data planes remain separate internally. #### Workstream C: compose PP with speculative decoding ##### C1. Base MTP draft-feedback synchronization Under MRV2 asynchronous scheduling, scheduler-side speculative token IDs are shape placeholders: their authoritative values remain in per-worker GPU request state. The speculative proposer runs on the last PP rank. Every stage's sampled/draft/sequence bookkeeping must nevertheless describe the same logical token sequence: the first stage materializes the correct sampled-plus-draft token IDs, while later stages consume the corresponding forward activations and attention metadata. Here `pp_feedback_step` means a local worker execute/control step that advances the `PPHandler` FIFO. It is not an EngineCore asynchronous batch-queue slot and is not advanced by a MoE DP dummy forward. #52295 implements the narrow synchronization piece. The last rank applies sampled state locally in feedback step `T`, runs proposal, retains its new draft state, and then publishes one feedback record to non-last ranks. The token wire payload is fixed at `[B, (K + 1) + K] = [B, 2K + 1]` (`int64` sampled plus draft columns), while the existing `[2, B]` (`int32`) sampled/rejected count collective remains. Draft synchronization therefore adds `K` token-ID columns per request but no new collective. Each non-last rank posts the matching receive in feedback step `T`, queues it with the saved row mapping, need mask, and slot-generation snapshot, and applies the surviving rows at feedback step `T + pp_size`. Sampled and draft rows use the same liveness/generation decision; invalid draft rows are compacted before index-copy because a `-1` destination is not valid for that operation. The association comes from FIFO feedback-step order and the saved step-`T` metadata, not from the composition of the current batch at `T + pp_size`. The required invariant is: > The last stage applies its sampling outcome and derived next-step drafts locally in feedback step `T` and publishes them as one causally consistent record. Every non-last stage posts the matching receive in step `T` and applies the stored live rows at feedback step `T + pp_size`, before that request's next verification input is prepared. #52295 should be treated as the base transport/state-synchronization change, not as the complete enablement of every MTP model. Its transport gate is PP plus any speculative configuration that has already passed validation, so this feedback mechanism should not be duplicated per speculative method. Broader model-specific work in #46994 includes PP capability declarations, model-specific projection paths, weight/embedding ownership, and a same-rank stale sparse-MLA buffer-reference fix. Those requirements should either land with the affected model or be guarded by an explicit support check; the same-rank buffer fix is distinct from the cross-rank dependency in C3. Fixed wire width also needs an explicit validity/padding protocol for a normal `[B, 1]` no-draft or prefill sampler source; `num_sampled` determines which sampled columns are valid. Existing #52295 coverage consists of two CPU/mock tests for payload splitting/event waiting and draft slot writeback. Real multi-rank communication, fixed-width send/receive, `T -> T + pp_size`, partial abort/reuse, and mixed prefill/decode are merge/enablement criteria, not established behavior. Delaying broadcast until after proposal may also change overlap, so validation must include TPOT and proposer latency. ##### C2. EAGLE3, DFlash, and DSpark auxiliary hidden states These methods require auxiliary target-model hidden states during proposal. MRV2 currently rejects EAGLE3, DFlash, and DSpark with PP before execution. If those guards were simply removed, each rank would capture only its local auxiliary outputs and a non-last rank would return ordinary `IntermediateTensors` without carrying those outputs, so the proposer on the last rank would still see incomplete state. For a configured set of auxiliary layers: 1. normalize each capture point to a global **activation-boundary ID** (`0` for the state before the first layer and `layer_idx + 1` for the state after that layer), including method-specific `+1` conversions; 2. map boundary IDs to the draft configuration's fixed slot order rather than numerically sorting IDs; 3. when an auxiliary state is produced, add it to the forward payload; 4. carry it through subsequent PP boundaries with `until_last` liveness; 5. combine upstream and last-rank-local states in configured slot order; 6. pass the ordered states to the proposer on the last PP rank. Auxiliary states are forward dependencies of the current microbatch, not delayed sampled-token feedback. They should therefore use the adjacent-rank forward plane and must not be added to the last-rank-to-non-last-ranks feedback broadcast. The schema must support zero, one, or multiple auxiliary tensors, and partition tests must cover auxiliary boundaries on the first, middle, and last PP ranks. Implementations that pack compatible states may use a stable `[N, slots, hidden]` layout where `N` is the padded execution row count, but correctness must not depend on all states having identical shapes. Persistent receive/pack buffers are a performance-phase optimization for avoiding per-step allocation and address changes under CUDA graphs. Transport is necessary but not sufficient to remove the current PP guards. Model-specific enablement must also normalize activation-boundary IDs and target layer counts to global (not stage-local) coordinates, validate draft embedding/head ownership on the last rank, and remove loader-level PP rejections only after the corresponding model path is tested. ##### C3. Index-sharing state across a PP cut Some models compute top-k routing/index information in one layer and reuse it in later layers. For example, an index-sharing pattern may contain one producing layer followed by layers that skip top-k computation and read a persistent buffer. If PP cuts between that producer and a consumer in the same reuse interval, a rank-local buffer on the downstream rank has not been populated for the current microbatch. The forward schema must then carry the active top-k buffer across one or more reuse-only stages until it is consumed or overwritten. At model/partition initialization, dependency analysis should determine whether a boundary crosses an index-reuse interval: - if it does not, no extra tensor is registered; - if it does, register the current contract—TP-replicated `[N, index_topk]` `torch.int32`, where `N` is the padded execution row count—and copy it into the downstream persistent shared buffer before model/graph execution; - tie buffer validity and lifetime to the forward microbatch/transport handle so data cannot leak between in-flight batches; - allow future model adapters to declare other trailing dimensions or dtypes without weakening this RFC's concrete acceptance contract. This cross-rank dependency is distinct from the stale-buffer-reference issue addressed by parts of #46994 when draft and target models share an indexer on the same rank. Both must be correct, but only the former requires PP-boundary transport. As an initial safety fallback, unsupported partitions may fail early with a precise error. The intended final behavior is to transport the dependency rather than permanently constraining PP cuts to index-reuse boundaries. #### Workstream D: PP-first DP/EP topology for multi-node serving This workstream is about **physical partition and placement order**, not a new DP load-balancing, dummy-forward, or drain protocol. Each request remains sticky to one logical DP lane, and that lane still traverses one complete PP pipeline. The proposal first assigns nodes to PP stages, then places the stage's DP/EP (and TP, when used) ranks inside that node. ##### D1. Background: why DP-first placement is suboptimal for multi-node MoE With a conventional DP-first placement, complete DP replicas are packed before moving to the next node. Consider two 8-GPU nodes with `PP=2`, `DP=8`, and `TP=1`: ```text default physical placement node 0: DP0{PP0,PP1} DP1{PP0,PP1} DP2{PP0,PP1} DP3{PP0,PP1} node 1: DP4{PP0,PP1} DP5{PP0,PP1} DP6{PP0,PP1} DP7{PP0,PP1} ``` This keeps several PP pipelines entirely inside a node, but the fixed-PP DP/EP domain spans both nodes. For MoE models, expert dispatch/combine is an all-to-all or all-gather/reduce-scatter style hot path repeated throughout the model. Sending that traffic across the inter-node fabric is substantially more topology-sensitive than keeping it on NVLink/NVSwitch. PP communication has a different shape: each logical DP lane sends activations across an ordered stage boundary, with small sampled/draft feedback in the reverse PP direction. This traffic is point-to-point or PP-scoped, regular, and can be overlapped with pipeline execution. It is therefore the preferable communication dimension to place across nodes. ##### D2. Proposed PP-first placement Place one complete PP stage's `DP x PCP x TP` footprint in a node-local topology domain before allocating the next PP stage: ```text PP-first physical placement node 0 / PP0: DP0 DP1 DP2 DP3 DP4 DP5 DP6 DP7 | | | | | | | | +--- matching cross-node PP lanes ---+ node 1 / PP1: DP0 DP1 DP2 DP3 DP4 DP5 DP6 DP7 ``` The resulting communication placement is: - `EP(pp)` stays inside the node containing that PP stage; - `TP(pp, dp, pcp)` also stays inside that stage's node-local domain; - `PP(dp, pcp, tp)` connects matching coordinates across nodes in stage order; - PP forward activations, optional sidecars from Workstream B, and small sampled/draft feedback are the steady-state model data that crosses nodes; - control-plane coordination may still cross nodes and is not the optimization target of this workstream. The physical placement can be PP-first without changing the logical identity of a DP lane. Scheduler, request, KV-cache, sampling, and speculative state remain owned by that lane; no request or KV state is migrated between DP lanes. ##### D3. Topology contract and scope The first rollout should target a uniform topology with one complete PP stage per node. Its contract is: - the stage footprint `DP x PCP x TP` fits completely in one node-local communication domain; - every EP and TP group is node-local; - each PP group contains matching `(dp, pcp, tp)` coordinates in increasing stage order; - every logical worker is placed exactly once, with no duplicated or missing device; - a requested placement that would spill an EP group across nodes fails before model execution; - disabling PP-first placement preserves the existing topology. Multiple complete stage blocks may share a node in a future extension, provided no EP/TP group is split across nodes. A stage footprint larger than one node, heterogeneous partial-stage placement, PCP+DP combinations that are otherwise unsupported, and elastic-EP composition are outside the initial scope. The existing DP/EP execution-order rules remain unchanged: ranks in a coupled EP domain must still enter model collectives consistently, and an idle logical DP lane still follows the existing dummy-execution behavior. These are compatibility requirements, not the feature proposed here. #### Cross-cutting correctness invariants 1. **Verification-state agreement:** every PP stage agrees on ordered request rows and logical token/position/spec-verification metadata; the first stage materializes the correct token IDs and downstream stages consume the corresponding stage-local forward state. 2. **Forward-dependency completeness:** the consumer of an auxiliary state or shared index sees the value produced for the same microbatch. 3. **Slot safety:** aborted, preempted, or replaced requests cannot consume delayed state from an earlier slot generation. 4. **Placement completeness:** every logical `(pp, dp, pcp, tp)` worker maps to exactly one physical device, and every selected device has exactly one owner. 5. **Topology locality:** in PP-first mode every EP/TP group is contained in one node-local communication domain, while PP groups connect matching coordinates in stage order. 6. **PP-lane isolation:** PP P2P and optional sidecars stay inside one logical DP lane and follow the per-edge transport plan. 7. **Feedback collective agreement:** every feedback participant uses group-identical row ordering, row count, dtype/shape, collective order, and whole-collective skip decisions for a feedback step. 8. **DP/EP execution compatibility:** changing physical placement does not change existing collective-order, dummy-execution, or execution-shape rules for a coupled EP domain. 9. **State isolation:** request, KV, sampling, and speculative state remain inside one sticky DP lane; PP transfer is not DP migration. 10. **Work conservation:** a soft balance target cannot indefinitely create empty PP phases while runnable work exists, and scheduler safety/fairness constraints take precedence. 11. **Feature transparency:** optional fields disabled add no bytes or collectives beyond the existing PP forward and sampled/count feedback paths; disabling PP-first placement preserves current topology. 12. **MRV1/non-PP compatibility:** this RFC does not change their scheduling or communication semantics. #### Rollout plan 1. Adapt the request-balancing prototype and scheduler tests from #50410 to the soft, work-conserving `WAITING`-admission MVP, then validate its policy/performance. 2. Introduce the ownership/adapter layer over the existing tensor-dict forward path and `PPHandler` feedback path without changing basic-generation behavior. 3. Land the base MTP draft-state synchronization from #52295, plus model-specific enablement or guards identified by #46994. 4. Add auxiliary-hidden-state descriptors and enable EAGLE3, DFlash, and DSpark model by model. 5. Add partition dependency analysis and cross-rank top-k/index transfer for index-sharing models. 6. Validate the PP-first multi-node topology contract, including node-local EP/TP groups and cross-node PP lanes. 7. Independently evaluate the static-wire/persistent-buffer transport performance phase. Steps that are independent may proceed in parallel, but every step should preserve the invariants above and keep unsupported combinations behind an early, actionable validation error. #### Compatibility and initial support limits - Target and draft model paths must explicitly satisfy PP capability, loader, projection, embedding/head ownership, and partition checks before their guard is removed. - Adaptive verification plus PP remains unsupported in the initial rollout. - Existing restrictions such as MRV2 PP with an external launcher, elastic EP with PP, and `PCP > 1` with `DP > 1` remain unchanged unless a separate RFC/PR addresses them. - `max_num_seqs` remains a per-EngineCore/per-DP-replica limit. - A draft model without its own embedding/head must either have a validated last-rank loading/aliasing path or fail early when the corresponding target component is a `PPMissingLayer`. - Initial PP-first support requires a uniform topology in which one complete `DP x PCP x TP` stage footprint fits inside one node-local communication domain. #### Alternatives considered 1. **Add model-specific tensors directly to each send/receive call.** This is smaller initially but duplicates buffer, ordering, and lifecycle logic and does not scale to the next optional state. 2. **Put every optional tensor in one always-present payload.** This simplifies branching but wastes memory/bandwidth and makes high-volume forward state share an unsuitable lifetime with small delayed token metadata. 3. **Use a separate collective for every field.** Simple semantically, but latency grows with features; #47686 shows why packing small PP feedback fields can matter. 4. **Force PP cuts to dependency boundaries.** Useful as a temporary guard, but reduces partition flexibility and can produce poor memory/compute balance. 5. **Send auxiliary hidden states directly from their producer to the last rank.** This creates a variable communication graph; forwarding through adjacent boundaries keeps ownership and ordering aligned with the existing pipeline. 6. **Keep DP-first physical placement.** This preserves current deployment behavior but can force EP traffic across nodes while underusing PP as the inter-node communication dimension. 7. **Use hierarchical cross-node EP collectives.** This may reduce the penalty but does not provide the same hard node-local EP/TP boundary and remains backend/topology dependent. 8. **Allow arbitrary heterogeneous stage placement immediately.** More flexible, but substantially harder to validate and reason about than a uniform one-stage-per-node first rollout. #### Evaluation plan **Correctness matrix** - PP sizes 2 and 4; DP sizes 1, 2, 4, and 8; TP 1/2 and representative EP configurations; - synchronous and asynchronous scheduling; eager and compiled/full-CUDA-graph execution; - no speculation, MTP, EAGLE3, DFlash, and DSpark; - speculative widths 1, 2, and 3, including no-draft/prefill feedback rows; - auxiliary layers before, on, and after PP boundaries; - PP cuts outside and inside an index-reuse interval; - burst admission, mixed prefill/decode, chunked prefill, preemption, abort storms, pause/resume, and request-slot reuse; - two 8-GPU nodes with `PP=2, DP=8, TP=1`; - two 8-GPU nodes with `PP=2, DP=4, TP=2`; - a representative `PP=4` topology; - both default DP-first and proposed PP-first physical placements. The model-level acceptance set should include: - Llama/Qwen EAGLE3 for global activation-boundary ID and configured-slot ordering; - DeepSeek V3.2 with a forced PP cut inside a producer-to-reuse interval; - DeepSeek V4 DSpark for post-mHC-mean auxiliary state; - Kimi K3 DSpark/EAGLE3 for model-specific attention-residual auxiliary state; - a draft model without its own embedding/head, covering either the validated last-rank loading path or the expected fail-fast error. Use synthetic/unit tests for exact transport contents, schema validation, boundary liveness, activation-boundary slot ordering, request generations, and topology membership. Add real multi-rank tests for `T -> T + pp_size` feedback cadence, abort/reuse filtering, fixed-width payloads, forward sidecars, and collective traces. Multi-node tests must collect actual node identities for every PP/DP/EP/TP group and prove that PP-first mode keeps EP/TP node-local. Representative end-to-end models should cover output parity and speculative acceptance; supported configurations should be compared with PP=1 using deterministic inputs where possible. Require no deadlock or collective-order mismatch under timeout/failure-injection tests. **Performance metrics** - requests and scheduled tokens per PP batch; - per-stage idle time and pipeline bubbles; - throughput, TTFT, and TPOT; - speculative acceptance rate and proposer latency; - PP bytes, collective/P2P count, and communication overlap; - CUDA-graph memory and capture/replay stability; - inter-node bytes attributed to PP forward/feedback versus EP/TP collectives; - EP all-to-all latency, PP overlap, node-local GPU utilization, and topology-induced idle time; - preemption count and KV-cache utilization. Optional transport disabled should have no material regression against current basic PP. Enabled configurations should be compared both before/after packing so communication optimizations remain evidence-driven. #### Related work - MRV2 pipeline bubble reduction and current PP/DP foundation: #42187 - Request-admission balancing prototype: #50410 - Isolated MTP draft-token synchronization: #52295 - Broader MTP-over-PP enablement and model-specific fixes: #46994 - Packed PP sampled/count/draft feedback draft experiment: #47686 - Async scheduling plan: #27679 - Persistent batch redesign: #23446 - Long-context optimized PP RFC: #41685 - Chunked pipeline parallel RFC: #33914 The long-context and chunked-PP RFCs focus on splitting long-context work, asynchronous P2P, and dynamic chunking. This RFC focuses on composing the existing MRV2 PP execution model with scheduler admission, speculative state, index-sharing dependencies, and a PP-first multi-node DP/EP topology. #### Open questions 1. Should the transport API extend `PPHandler` and `IntermediateTensors`, or should both become clients of a new internal `PPTransport` owner? 2. Which small fields should be packed, and what static layout/versioning is needed for full CUDA graphs? 3. Should auxiliary hidden states remain individually keyed by activation-boundary/slot or use one packed tensor plus offsets? 4. Should cross-boundary index state be transported for all supported models, or should the first rollout reject unsafe partition cuts? 5. Should PP admission balance requests, tokens, estimated compute, or a hybrid, and should it be opt-in initially? 6. Should PP-first placement be explicit-only at first, or selected automatically when the stage footprint matches node capacity? 7. Must the initial topology require exactly one PP stage per node, or may a node host multiple complete stage blocks? 8. If an EP domain cannot fit in one node, should configuration fail, fall back to DP-first placement, or require an explicitly selected hierarchical EP mode? 9. Which feature combinations are required before removing the current PP validation guards for EAGLE3, DFlash, and DSpark? ### Feedback Period. 2026-08-18 through 2026-09-01. ### CC List. @njhill @WoosukKwon @robertgshaw2-redhat @heheda12345 @youkaichao @eastwood-c @ChihayaK @yewentao256 ### Any Other Things. The author can provide scheduler traces, device profiles, representative PP partition layouts, and acceptance-rate results for the proposed combinations. Feedback is especially welcome on the transport ownership boundary, the minimum support matrix for the first rollout, and whether index-sharing dependencies should initially be transported or guarded by partition validation.

signal.title: [Feature]: Map unsupported reasoning_effort values to the nearest level the chat template accepts
signal.text: ## 🚀 The feature, motivation and pitch Some chat templates accept only a subset of the reasoning effort ladder and raise a Jinja error on anything else. For example, the official `Qwen/Qwen3.8-27B` template validates `reasoning_effort` directly against `('xhigh', 'medium', 'low')`, so a request with `high` returns HTTP 400: `Unexpected reasoning effort high. Supported types are xhigh (default), medium, and low.` Meanwhile the `ChatCompletionRequest.reasoning_effort` field accepts the full ladder (`none`/`minimal`/`low`/`medium`/`high`/`xhigh`/`max`), and OpenAI-compatible clients — agent harnesses especially — routinely send `high` or `minimal`. The request validates at the API layer, then fails at template render time. Today the only ways around this are patching vLLM, forking the chat template, or rewriting requests in a fronting proxy. Proposal: let the operator declare the levels the served model's template accepts, and have vLLM remap any other requested value to the nearest supported level: ```bash vllm serve Qwen/Qwen3.8-27B \ --supported-reasoning-efforts low medium xhigh \ --reasoning-effort-rounding down ``` Semantics (on the ladder `minimal < low < medium < high < xhigh < max`): - `--reasoning-effort-rounding down` (default): highest supported level at or below the requested one; if nothing is at or below, the lowest supported level. With the set above: `high` → `medium`, `minimal` → `low`. - `--reasoning-effort-rounding up`: lowest supported level at or above the requested one; if nothing is at or above, the highest supported level. With the set above: `high` → `xhigh`. - `none` (reasoning disabled) always passes through and cannot be listed in the supported set — the mapping never toggles thinking on or off. - Flags unset → passthrough, exactly today's behavior. - Each distinct (requested → effective) remap is logged once as a warning. The mapping applies at the serving layer (Chat Completions, Responses, and Anthropic Messages APIs), so every derivation path a client uses converges on the same normalization before the template renders. There is in-tree precedent for the underlying concept: the Harmony path keeps its own private `REASONING_EFFORT` mapping in `vllm/entrypoints/openai/parser/harmony_utils.py` because GPT-OSS supports a subset too. This proposal makes the capability declarative and general instead of per-model-family. I have a working implementation (small: one new helper module, two frontend flags, wiring in the chat/responses serving layers, unit tests, docs) and will open a PR if this is welcome. ## Alternatives - **Explicit mapping strings** (`--reasoning-effort-map high=medium,...`): more flexible but more configuration surface and easy to misconfigure; the supported-set + rounding-direction form covers the real cases with two short flags. Could be added later if a concrete need appears. - **Fix in each chat template**: templates come from model repos; operators can't always change them, and every template author would have to re-implement tolerant handling. - **Client-side/proxy rewriting**: works but must be re-implemented per client/proxy and per derivation path (effort can be derived from thinking budgets, explicit fields, etc.). - **Do nothing**: requests keep failing at render time with a template error that's hard to trace back to the offending request field. ## Additional context Observed with an OpenAI-compatible agent harness driving a Qwen3.8 model: the harness derives `reasoning_effort` values (`high`, `minimal`) that the template rejects, and affected turns fail with the HTTP 400 above until the operator patches the server or the requests. Verified end-to-end on `Qwen/Qwen3.8-27B` (BF16): stock serve 400s on `high` as quoted; with `--supported-reasoning-efforts low medium xhigh` the same request returns 200 with `high` remapped to `medium` (rounding=`down`) or `xhigh` (rounding=`up`, confirmed via the injected reasoning-instructions block in the prompt token count), one warning logged per distinct remap. Also verified `minimal` → `low` (400 → 200) on a community NVFP4 re-quantization of the same model. Note: some third-party re-uploads ship modified templates that alias `high`→`xhigh` themselves; the official template does not, and `minimal`/`max` fail on both.

signal.title: fix: propagate precompiled wheel variant lookup failure instead of falling back
signal.text: Fixes vllm-project/vllm#52544 ## Summary For Python-only builds, when the precompiled-wheel metadata lookup for the selected CUDA variant fails, `setup.py` fell back to the root/default variant index. Nothing downstream checks that the fallback wheel matches the CUDA variant that was selected (or auto-detected) — the issue reporter hit exactly this: PyTorch CUDA 12.9 selected `cu129`, its metadata lookup failed, and the fallback picked a native artifact requiring CUDA 13. The fix propagates the variant lookup failure instead of retrying the root index: once a variant is selected, only that variant's metadata is fetched. A wrong-CUDA wheel is worse than an install failure, because it fails far from the config that caused it. ## Verification - `setup.py` parses cleanly (`ast.parse`). - No other code path depends on the removed `try_default`/`download_filename` initializer — `download_filename` is still assigned in the wheel-selection branches that follow.

signal.title: [ROCm][Model][Bugfix] Enable GLM-5.2-MXFP4 on the deepseek_v32 path and fix sparse attention correctness
signal.text: ## Purpose Enables GLM-5.2 (`GlmMoeDsaForCausalLM`) end-to-end on `vllm/models/deepseek_v32/amd/` for gfx942/gfx950. Routing is opt-in via `--model-class-overrides`; the registry entry is unchanged, so the default path for GLM-5.2 and DeepSeek-V3.2 is untouched. The following issues were also fixed as a result of this overall enablement since it surfaced dormant bugs from a prior deepseek_v32 porting work: - **`launch_pdl` forwarded to a Triton runtime that doesn't accept it** — the shared `common/kernels.py` passed this CUDA-only kwarg unconditionally; ROCm's Triton rejects it by name even when `False`, so the engine died at startup with `KeyError`. Now passed only when the platform actually supports PDL. - **fp4 bmm invoked with mismatched positional args** — the output tensor landed in the kernel's `dtype` slot (`Expected 'Optional[int]' for 'dtype' but found Tensor`). Routed through the existing `rocm_aiter_ops.batched_gemm_a16wfp4` wrapper rather than calling aiter directly, so the argument contract lives in one place. - **fp4 MLA bmm silently wrong for non-power-of-two K** — `batched_gemm_a16wfp4` only supports power-of-two K, and returns wrong values without erroring otherwise. GLM-5.2's `qk_nope_head_dim=192` lands in the unsupported set; DeepSeek-V3.2's 128 does not. Guarded on both `qk_nope_head_dim` and `kv_lora_rank` to fall back to the fp8 bmm, with a warning. `W_K`/`W_K_scale` are also made contiguous after the transpose, which otherwise produced NaN. - **Indexer-K cache written in the plain layout while its reader expects the shuffled one** — affects DeepSeek-V3.2 identically, not just GLM-5.2. The AMD path writes this cache from the shared `fused_norm_rope`, which only implemented `[n_blocks, blk, head_dim]`, while the reader selects `SHUFFLE` above block size 1: the write kept storing row-major, but the reader expected shuffled, so the indexer scored garbage K and output degenerated once a sequence exceeded `index_topk=2048`, with no error raised. Refactored so the shared kernel stays platform-agnostic — it writes whichever layout the cache reports via a new `uses_shuffled_layout` property — and the AMD-specific shuffled write (`[n_blocks, blk/16, head_dim/16, 16, 16]`, used above block size 1) lives in the AMD backend. The base class returns `False`, so CUDA is unchanged. - **Sparse-MLA block sizes narrowed instead of extended** — the ported backends replaced the inherited `get_supported_kernel_block_sizes()` with `[16, 32]`, which made `select_common_block_size` silently downgrade a requested 64 to 32 via its largest-divisor fallback. Now concatenated with the base list. - **Kernel tests gated on `is_cuda()` and running against dims that matched neither model** — the tests were skipped entirely on CDNA. The gate is now `supports_fp8()`, so the suite runs on gfx950. The hardcoded attention dims were written as if one set served both GLM-5.2 and DeepSeek-V3.2, which it did not; they are now taken from each model's published config and parametrized over both. ## Test Plan Server: VLLM_ROCM_USE_AITER=1 \ HF_HUB_OFFLINE=1 SAFETENSORS_FAST_GPU=1 \ vllm serve /path-to-your/GLM-5.2-MXFP4 \ --model-class-overrides '{"GlmMoeDsaForCausalLM": "vllm.models.deepseek_v32:DeepseekV32ForCausalLM"}' \ --tensor-parallel-size 8 \ --kv-cache-dtype auto \ --max-model-len 65536 \ --no-enable-prefix-caching \ --trust-remote-code \ --port 8000 Variants: --kv-cache-dtype fp8 for the fp8 KV row; --block-size {16,64} for the block-size matrix. Drop --model-class-overrides to run the legacy deepseek_v2 path for comparison. Accuracy: lm_eval --model local-completions \ --model_args "model=/models/GLM-5.2-MXFP4,base_url=http://localhost:8000/v1/completions,num_concurrent=32,tokenized_requests=False,max_retries=3,timeout=3600" \ --tasks gsm8k --num_fewshot 5 --gen_kwargs max_gen_toks=2048 --limit 200 Throughput: vllm bench serve --backend vllm --model /shareddata/models/GLM-5.2-MXFP4 \ --dataset-name random --random-input-len 4096 --random-output-len 1024 \ --num-prompts 200 --max-concurrency 32 --ignore-eos --port 8000 \ --save-result --result-filename glm52_v32amd_bench.json Kernel unit tests: pytest tests/kernels/test_fused_deepseek_v32_norm_rope.py -v ## Test Result **gsm8k** — GLM-5.2 200 samples, 5-shot, `exact_match`, `deepseek_v32` AMD path | KV cache | Before (flexible / strict) | After (flexible / strict) | |-------------|----------------------------|------------------------------| | auto (bf16) | 0.0000 / 0.0000 | **0.9400 / 0.9400** ± 0.0168 | | fp8 | 0.0000 / 0.0000 \* | **0.9350 / 0.9350** ± 0.0175 | \* Not separately measured. fp8 KV goes through the same absorbed-weight bmm where the bug was, so it fails identically; only the bf16 run was evaluated pre-fix.

signal.title: [Bugfix][LoRA] Add embedding_modules for Qwen3.5 CausalLM
signal.text: Register embed_tokens and lm_head so PEFT adapters that target embedding/output heads pass unexpected-module validation, matching Qwen3 and Qwen3-MoE. ## Purpose Fixes https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/48934. `Qwen3_5ForCausalLMBase` implements `SupportsLoRA` but did not define `embedding_modules`. Loading a PEFT adapter whose `target_modules` include `embed_tokens` / `lm_head` fails unexpected-module validation in `LoRAModel.from_local_checkpoint`, even though the same adapters work on Qwen3 / Qwen3-MoE. This PR adds `embedding_modules` for `embed_tokens` and `lm_head` on `Qwen3_5ForCausalLMBase`, matching `Qwen3ForCausalLM` / `Qwen3MoeForCausalLM`. Fixex #48934,Related prior work for the Qwen2/3 family: #33234 / #29816. This is not a duplicate; Qwen3.5 still lacked the registration. ## Test Plan - `ruff check vllm/model_executor/models/qwen3_5.py` - `ruff format --check vllm/model_executor/models/qwen3_5.py` - Load a Qwen3.5-compatible LoRA with `embed_tokens` / `lm_head` in `target_modules` and `enable_lora=True`; confirm `from_local_checkpoint` / engine init no longer raises unexpected-module `ValueError`. ## Test Result **Before:** adapters targeting `embed_tokens` / `lm_head` fail with unexpected-module validation because those names are missing from Qwen3.5 `expected_lora_modules`. **After:** - `embedding_modules` registered on `Qwen3_5ForCausalLMBase` (same mapping as Qwen3). - `ruff check` / `ruff format --check` on the touched file: passed. --- <details> <summary> Essential Elements of an Effective PR Description Checklist </summary> aligns Qwen3.5 with existing Qwen3 LoRA embedding support - [√] The purpose of the PR, such as "Fix some issue (link existing issues this PR will resolve)". - - [x] The test plan, such as providing test command. - [x] The test results, such as pasting the results comparison before and after, or e2e results - [x] (Optional) The necessary documentation update, such as updating `supported_models.md` and `examples` for a new model. - N/A: aligns Qwen3.5 with existing Qwen3 LoRA embedding support; no new model docs. </details>

signal.title: [Bugfix][Multimodal] Enable Qwen3.8-27B LM-only mode without vision tower
signal.text: ## Purpose This PR targets Qwen3.8-27B language-model-only deployments. Qwen3.8-27B is served through vLLM's Qwen3.5-compatible hybrid model path. When `--language-model-only` is enabled, all image and video limits are zero, so the vision tower cannot execute. Before this change, the shared model path could still construct and load the vision tower, and the runtime could still prepare encoder CUDA graphs even though no configured modality could use them. That unnecessary work is particularly costly for a 27B deployment: it consumes GPU memory that should be available to the language model and KV cache, and it can add avoidable initialization and CUDA-graph setup to a text-only serving path. This change: - Uses a metadata-only vision-tower placeholder in the Qwen3.5-compatible path used by Qwen3.8-27B when image and video limits are both zero. - Preserves the tower metadata needed by the language-model code path without allocating vision parameters or buffers. - Adds an explicit multimodal-encoder capability check and skips encoder CUDA graph setup when no configured modality can execute the encoder. - Covers both dense and MoE variants of the shared Qwen3.5-compatible path with regression tests. This is not a new model implementation. It makes the existing hybrid execution path honor text-only mode for Qwen3.8-27B and avoids allocating components that cannot execute in that deployment. ## Test Plan Unit tests: ```bash .venv/bin/python -m pytest \ tests/model_executor/test_qwen3_5_language_model_only.py \ tests/multimodal/test_registry.py::test_supports_multimodal_encoder \ tests/v1/cudagraph/test_encoder_cudagraph.py::test_embedding_only_mode_skips_encoder_cudagraph_manager \ -q ``` Regression vehicle and runtime smoke test on an NVIDIA GeForce RTX 4090: - Model: `Qwen/Qwen3.5-0.8B`, the smallest available checkpoint exercising the same Qwen3.5-compatible hybrid implementation path. - Run once with `language_model_only=True` and once without the flag. - Generate a short text response from each configuration. The Qwen3.5-0.8B test is a minimal regression vehicle for the Qwen3.8-27B execution path. It is not intended to represent a Qwen3.8-27B memory measurement. ## Test Result Unit tests: ```text 11 passed, 14 warnings in 49.20s ``` Both runtime configurations loaded the real `Qwen/Qwen3.5-0.8B` checkpoint and returned text. The LM-only run logged: ```text All limits of multimodal modalities supported by the model are set to 0, running in text-only mode. ``` Example generated response from the LM-only run: ```text The sky appears blue because the atmosphere scatters shorter wavelengths of light (blue) more effectively than ... ``` Memory comparison (same model and prompt; values are rounded from vLLM logs): | Configuration | Model loading | KV cache | | --- | ---: | ---: | | Default multimodal | 1.72 GiB | 34.70 GiB | | `language_model_only=True` | 1.53 GiB | 36.17 GiB | | Difference | **0.19 GiB less** | **1.47 GiB more available** | This measurement is from the 0.8B regression vehicle and is not presented as a 27B projection. It demonstrates the allocation that the LM-only path removes; for Qwen3.8-27B, the value is avoiding that unnecessary vision allocation and encoder setup within a much tighter model-serving memory budget. No model-accuracy evaluation was added because this change only controls multimodal module construction and encoder CUDA-graph setup; the language-model weights and text generation path are unchanged. A real-weight generation smoke test was run for both configurations. ## Duplicate-work Check No issue was assigned to this PR. Searches of open vLLM pull requests and issues for Qwen3.8-27B, Qwen3.5, `language_model_only`, vision tower, and multimodal encoder found no existing PR covering this fix. Related Qwen3.8-27B reports, including [#52654](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/52654) and [#52682](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/52682), address multimodal encoder TP behavior and CUDA-graph startup hangs rather than unnecessary vision-tower construction in LM-only mode. ## Documentation No documentation update is required; the existing supported-models documentation already describes text-only mode via `--language-model-only`. ## AI Assistance AI assistance was used to inspect the branch, draft this description, run the unit tests, run real-weight Qwen3.5 generation, and measure the memory difference. The human submitter must review every changed line and verify the reported test and runtime results before submitting the PR.

signal.title: [Feature]: Support per-request dynamic LoRA scale
signal.text: ### 🚀 The feature, motivation and pitch Currently `LoRARequest.lora_scale` is fixed at request creation and baked into the CUDA graph / kernel as a scalar. This prevents: - same-adapter requests in one batch from using different strengths; - adjusting LoRA strength mid-generation. A real ASR service works around this by baking scale into separate adapter copies (one slot per scale). This wastes slots and limits scale to discrete presets. **Proposal:** Add `LoRAScaleState` — a per-request `UvaBackedTensor` (`[max_num_reqs]`) following `SamplingStates`, passed to the LoRA kernel along with `token_to_req`. Effective scale = `base_scale * request_lora_scales[token_to_req[token_idx]]`. No per-token memory, CUDA-graph-compatible. **Evaluation (real adapter + WER A/B):** | Condition | CN mean \|B-A\| | EN mean \|B-A\| | | --- | --- | --- | | off (noise floor) | 0.022% | — | | 1.0 pre-fix | 17.184% | — | | 1.0 post-fix | 0.038% | 0.028% | - 4 adapter slots → 1 slot. - Arbitrary continuous scale values. - Two bugs found & fixed: CUDA graph captured the scale-free kernel variant (`tl.constexpr`), and the all-ones buffer wasn't refreshed. ### Alternatives - **Baking scale into separate adapter copies** (current workaround) — consumes one adapter slot per scale, limited to discrete presets such as `LORA_SCALES=0.5,0.7,0.9,1.0`. - **Storing a per-token scale array** — would require more GPU memory (e.g. 128 KB per batch vs 1 KB per request) and does not follow vLLM V1 persistent-batch style. ### Additional context - Full per-test-set breakdowns and logs are available on request. - Happy to open a PR if this direction is reasonable. ### Before submitting a new issue... - [x] Make sure you already searched for relevant issues, and asked the chatbot living at the bottom right corner of the [documentation page](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/), which can answer lots of frequently asked questions.

signal.title: [Bug] DeepseekV4 cannot start on sm_121 (GB10): unguarded DeepGEMM call, and CutlassScaledMM.is_supported() ignores compute capability
signal.text: ### Your current environment - vLLM `0.26.1rc1.dev608+g99a10304d` (container image, aarch64) - 2× NVIDIA GB10 (**sm_121**, 121 GiB unified memory each), CUDA 13.0, driver 580.173.02 - Two-node TP=2 via the built-in multi-node `mp` executor (`--nnodes 2 --node-rank {0,1} --master-addr … --distributed-executor-backend mp`, rank 1 `--headless`) - Model: `MJPansa/DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731-NVFP4` (mixed precision: routed experts NVFP4, attention / shared experts / head not quantized) - `VLLM_USE_DEEP_GEMM=0` and `VLLM_MOE_USE_DEEP_GEMM=0` are set Other models start and serve fine on the same two-node setup with the same image (Qwen3-235B-A22B-NVFP4, Mistral-Small-4-119B, Qwen3.8-27B-FP8), so the cluster wiring itself is good. ### 🐛 Describe the bug DeepseekV4 cannot start on sm_121. There are two separate architecture gates that report "supported" and then fail inside compiled kernels. **1. `mhc_pre_broadcast_tilelang` calls DeepGEMM unconditionally** `vllm/model_executor/kernels/mhc/tilelang.py` has three call sites for `tf32_hc_prenorm_gemm`. Two of them are guarded: ```python use_deep_gemm = is_deep_gemm_supported() ... if use_deep_gemm: tf32_hc_prenorm_gemm(...) else: _tilelang_hc_prenorm_gemm(...) ``` The third one, inside `mhc_pre_broadcast_tilelang` (the first-layer 2-D input path taken from `models/deepseek_v4/nvidia/model.py`), is not: ```python from vllm.utils.deep_gemm import tf32_hc_prenorm_gemm tf32_hc_prenorm_gemm( residual_flat, fn_broadcast, gemm_out_mul, gemm_out_sqrsum, n_splits, ) ``` On sm_121 this aborts during `determine_available_memory`: ``` RuntimeError: Worker failed with error 'Assertion error (/workspace/.deps/deepgemm-src/csrc/apis/hyperconnection.hpp:56): Unsupported architecture' ``` The shipped DeepGEMM extension only contains kernels for two architectures: ``` $ strings vllm/third_party/deep_gemm/_C.cpython-312-aarch64-linux-gnu.so | grep -oE 'sm[0-9]{2,3}' | sort -u sm100 sm90 ``` Note this happens **even with `VLLM_USE_DEEP_GEMM=0`**. That env var does work — `is_deep_gemm_supported()` returns `False` with it set and `True` without it — but this call site never consults it. A fix that works: guard the call and fall back to `_torch_hc_prenorm_gemm`, which already exists in the same file and implements exactly this contract (`out[0] = x.float() @ fn.t()`, `sqrsum[0] = x.float().square().sum(-1)`); the broadcast shapes line up as-is. It requires a single split, so `n_splits` has to be forced to 1 on the fallback path before the output tensors are allocated. With that patch the model loads all 48 shards and gets past this point. **2. `CutlassScaledMM.is_supported()` ignores compute capability** Past the first issue, DeepseekV4's attention input projections fail: ``` File "vllm/models/deepseek_v4/attention.py", line 493, in _run_parallel_input_projections File "vllm/model_executor/layers/quantization/fp8.py", line 461, in apply File "vllm/model_executor/kernels/linear/scaled_mm/BlockScaledMMLinearKernel.py", line 132, in apply_weights File "vllm/model_executor/kernels/linear/scaled_mm/cutlass.py", line 320, in apply_block_scaled_mm RuntimeError: dispatch_scaled_mm, /workspace/csrc/libtorch_stable/quantization/w8a8/cutlass/c3x/scaled_mm_helper.hpp:17 ``` The selection gate in `kernels/linear/scaled_mm/cutlass.py` is: ```python @classmethod def is_supported(cls, compute_capability: int | None = None) -> tuple[bool, str | None]: if not current_platform.is_cuda(): return False, "requires CUDA." return True, None ``` `compute_capability` is accepted and never used, so the CUTLASS c3x kernel is selected on any CUDA device and then rejects sm_121 in the C++ dispatcher. A Triton implementation exists in the same directory, but `use_triton` on `BlockScaledMMLinearKernel` only affects the input-quantisation step, not the matmul, and there is no env var to override the backend choice. ### Suggested fix Both gates should consult compute capability rather than assuming Hopper/datacenter-Blackwell: - `CutlassScaledMM.is_supported()` should return `False` on architectures without the compiled c3x kernels so selection can fall through to the Triton kernel. - `is_deep_gemm_supported()` should reflect the architectures actually compiled into the extension (currently sm90/sm100), not just the env var — otherwise every DeepGEMM call site needs to be individually correct. - `mhc_pre_broadcast_tilelang` should be guarded like its two siblings regardless. Happy to open a PR for the `mhc_pre_broadcast_tilelang` guard if that shape of fix is acceptable.

signal.title: [Build][AMD] Update triton_kernels pin for RDNA MXFP4 matmul_ogs config
signal.text: Advances the ROCm triton_kernels pin to 74e4569a70, which backports upstream Triton PR #10810 ("[AMD][kernels] Improve MXFP4 matmul_ogs config on RDNA"). Avoids register spilling in the MXFP4 MoE GEMMs on RDNA. ## Purpose Advances the ROCm `triton_kernels` pin in `cmake/external_projects/triton_kernels.cmake` from `0f380657` to `74e4569a70`, picking up the RDNA MXFP4 `matmul_ogs` configuration change. - Upstream Triton PR: https://github.com/triton-lang/triton/pull/10810 - ROCm backport (the commit this pin now points at): https://github.com/ROCm/triton/pull/951 **Why it matters.** On RDNA the current pin selects `block_m = 128` tiles for the MXFP4 MoE GEMMs. The fp32 accumulator alone is `BLOCK_M × BLOCK_N` registers, which at that tile size consumes half of the 256-VGPR wave32 budget before any operand is loaded. Register demand exceeds the architectural cap, the compiler spills to scratch memory, and the spills land inside the K-loop where the cost is paid on every iteration. WMMA instruction counts are unchanged — the arithmetic is identical and the extra time is pure spill overhead. The backported configuration sets `block_m` explicitly for MXFP4 on RDNA, so the spilling tiles are never built. This is a pin bump only. The kernel selection logic is ROCm's backport of upstream work; no vLLM code is changed beyond the pinned SHA. ## Test Plan `gpt-oss-20b` (MXFP4 MoE) on RDNA, TP=1. ```bash vllm bench throughput \ --model openai/gpt-oss-20b --max_model_len 4096 --trust-remote-code \ --dataset-name sharegpt --dataset-path ShareGPT_V3_unfiltered_cleaned_split.json \ --num_prompts 1000 --tensor_parallel_size 1 --gpu-memory-utilization 0.8 ``` Register and spill counts read from `.vgpr_count` / `.vgpr_spill_count` in the compiled `.amdgcn` products, selecting the autotune-chosen variant by `num_warps`. ## Test Result Confirmed the performance gain on RDNA that the linked PRs describe. Throughput improved and no remaining kernel spills observed.

### 🐛 Describe the bug ## Summary When vLLM is started with `--cudagraph-metrics`, CUDA Graph execution is active and normal periodic statistics are logged, but the documented CUDA Graph statistics table is never emitted. The issue reproduces with: - vLLM 0.27.1 - NVIDIA L40S - `VLLM_LOGGING_LEVEL=INFO` - `ObservabilityConfig.cudagraph_metrics=True` - `FULL_AND_PIECEWISE` CUDA Graph mode - sustained inference load spanning multiple logging intervals - stdout and stderr captured together The server remains healthy and all requests complete successfully. This is an observability bug rather than an inference correctness bug: CUDA Graph execution works, but the metrics enabled by `--cudagraph-metrics` are silently absent. ## Environment - vLLM: `0.27.1` - Python: `3.12.13` - PyTorch: `2.13.0+cu130` - CUDA runtime reported by PyTorch: `13.0` - GPU: NVIDIA L40S - NVIDIA driver: `595.71.05` - Model: `Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B` - Engine: V1 - CUDA Graph mode: `FULL_AND_PIECEWISE` - Logging level: explicitly set to `INFO` The server system fingerprint was: ```text vllm-0.27.1-55fa4e7f ``` ## Expected behavior According to `ObservabilityConfig.cudagraph_metrics`, enabling CUDA Graph metrics should report: - unpadded token count - padded token count - number of padding tokens - runtime CUDA Graph dispatch mode - observed frequency The implementation also defines a log table beginning with: ```text **CUDAGraph Config Settings:** - Mode: ... - Capture sizes: ... **CUDAGraph Stats:** | Unpadded Tokens | Padded Tokens | Num Paddings | Runtime Mode | Count | ``` Relevant source: - https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/main/vllm/config/observability.py - https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/main/vllm/compilation/cuda_graph.py At least one CUDA Graph statistics table should be emitted during or after the sustained workload. ## Actual behavior The logs confirm that the option is enabled: ```text non-default args: { ... 'cudagraph_metrics': True, ... } ``` The engine configuration also confirms it: ```text ObservabilityConfig( ... cudagraph_metrics=True, ... ) ``` CUDA Graph capture succeeds: ```text Graph capturing finished in 1 secs, took 0.09 GiB ``` Normal periodic statistics are emitted at INFO level: ```text Engine 000: Avg prompt throughput: 2734.6 tokens/s, Avg generation throughput: 2234.3 tokens/s, Running: 15 reqs, Waiting: 1 reqs, GPU KV cache usage: 0.9%, Prefix cache hit rate: 0.0% Engine 000: Avg prompt throughput: 989.1 tokens/s, Avg generation throughput: 819.1 tokens/s, Running: 0 reqs, Waiting: 0 reqs, GPU KV cache usage: 0.0%, Prefix cache hit rate: 0.0% ``` However, the combined stdout/stderr log contains none of the following: ```text CUDAGraph Config Settings CUDAGraph Stats Unpadded Tokens Padded Tokens Runtime Mode ``` The server remains healthy and all inference requests succeed. ## Why this does not appear to be a logging configuration issue The reproduction explicitly rules out the common configuration explanations: | Possible explanation | Result | |---|---| | `--cudagraph-metrics` was not enabled | The parsed CLI arguments show `cudagraph_metrics=True` | | `ObservabilityConfig` did not receive the option | `ObservabilityConfig.cudagraph_metrics=True` appears in the engine log | | Log level was too restrictive | `VLLM_LOGGING_LEVEL=INFO` is explicitly set | | INFO logging was disabled | Normal periodic engine statistics appear at INFO | | The logging interval was not reached | The workload runs continuously for 25 seconds and is followed by another request after 12 seconds | | Output was written to a different stream | stdout and stderr are redirected into the same log | | CUDA Graph execution was inactive | Graph capture completes successfully | | The server failed during the test | Requests succeed and `/health` remains available | The issue was also observed with asynchronous scheduling disabled, so it does not appear specific to the async scheduler. ## Reproduction Download [repro_cudagraph_metrics.sh](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/31173012/repro_cudagraph_metrics.sh) Run it with: ```bash chmod +x repro_cudagraph_metrics.sh PYTHON_BIN="$(command -v python)" GPU=0 ./repro_cudagraph_metrics.sh ``` The script exits with status `1` when the bug is reproduced. ## Reproduction result On vLLM 0.27.1 with an NVIDIA L40S: ```text Server is healthy Completed requests: 256 Errors: 0 Logging-trigger request HTTP status: 200 BUG REPRODUCED --cudagraph-metrics was enabled and normal INFO logging ran, but no CUDA Graph runtime statistics were emitted. ``` ## Additional control runs The same missing-output behavior was observed in both configurations: 1. Default asynchronous scheduling. 2. Explicit synchronous scheduling using `--no-async-scheduling`. Therefore, the missing statistics do not appear to be caused solely by asynchronous scheduling. ## Related context - CUDA Graph logging implementation: https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/main/vllm/compilation/cuda_graph.py - Observability configuration: https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/main/vllm/config/observability.py - Original CUDA Graph logging PR: https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/29825 - Draft Prometheus CUDA Graph counter PR: https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/37576 PR #37576 concerns adding a Prometheus counter. This report concerns the existing verbose text table controlled by `--cudagraph-metrics`. ### Before submitting a new issue... - [x] Make sure you already searched for relevant issues, and asked the chatbot living at the bottom right corner of the [documentation page](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/), which can answer lots of frequently asked questions.

signal.title: support rl feature : weight checker
signal.text: ## Purpose In the RL training loop: start_weight_update → update_weights* → finish_weight_update, we need to confirm that after the training side pushes/synchronizes the Actor weights to the rollout inference engine, the weights held by the engine are indeed consistent with what we intended to push. Before the training loop begins, check the correctness of the weight-update function to avoid off-policy training crashes. To confirm that this weight update actually landed and was not corrupted or partially written, a reproducible verification mechanism is needed. **weight_checker** is designed for exactly this: it computes a **SHA-256 checksum for each weight tensor of the model** and takes **snapshots (snapshot)** and **comparisons (compare)** before and after the update, so that you can verify ahead of time "whether the weights actually changed / whether they are complete." The four actions that weight_checker depends on: * **snapshot**: Compute a SHA-256 value of the current weights and store it as a baseline * **compare**: Recompute the current SHA-256 values Gang compare them with the snapshot, returning `match` + `mismatches` * **checksum**: Return the current per-tensor SHA-256 values without storing them (idempotent) * **reset**: Randomize the weights after a snapshot, to set up detection of whether a later weight update was correct #[52689](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/52689) ## Test Plan A single parameterized test file drives the dev server for each TP setting and verifies: -snapshot returns a structured response with a positive tensor count, and repeated snapshots are consistent. -compare requires a prior snapshot (400 otherwise), matches when weights are unchanged, and still matches after a sleep/wake cycle and after a generate request. -checksum returns per-tensor 64-character SHA-256 digests, is stable across calls, and does not clobber an existing snapshot. -reset rewrite the model weight to check update is correct. -error handling rejects missing/unknown actions cleanly while /health stays up. -world size matches the configured tensor_parallel_size. | Test group | Functional points covered | Priority | | --- | --- | --- | | Snapshot | world size, snapshot behavior | P0 | | Compare | state handling during comparison | P0 | | Checksum | checksum stability and behavior | P0 | | Reset | reset behavior | P0 | | Errors | invalid-request handling | P1 | ## Test Result default test tp=1 and 2 signal.title: [Feature]: Low-overhead asynchronous early-exit checks & KV-cache reclamation for Continuous Batching
signal.text: ### 🚀 The feature, motivation and pitch Problem Statement In high-throughput production environments running long-context agent loops or strict JSON-enforcement pipelines, models frequently burn a significant portion of generation cycles on post-plateau tail-tokens (e.g., polite wrappers, redundant formatting) after the core semantic task is complete. While stop_strings and custom LogitsProcessor hooks exist, evaluating them per-step in Python introduces severe bottlenecks: CPU-GPU Sync & GIL Contenter: Per-step synchronous callbacks disrupt the execution loop, create heavy interpreter friction, and degrade throughput at scale (batch size > 64). Even in Python-heavy orchestration stacks, this creates unacceptable micro-lags. KV-Cache Bloat & Fragmentation: Finished or logically complete sequences linger in the active batch until the explicit stop token hits or max tokens are reached, occupying precious blocks in PagedAttention and artificially inflating latency for concurrent requests. An Economic Perspective In high-volume enterprise deployments (e.g., fintech, customer ops, logistics), long-context generation loops routinely burn 20–30% of output tokens on post-plateau tail generation. For enterprise clients processing tens of millions of requests monthly, this translates to hundreds of thousands of dollars in wasted infrastructure costs annually, plus artificial latency inflation due to occupied KV-cache slots. Has anyone in the community tackled token overconsumption and mid-batch memory reclamation from a production-economy standpoint? How are large-scale deployments justifying or mitigating these dead compute cycles today? Proposed Solution Introduce a lightweight, optimized mechanism at the scheduler level to handle dynamic early-exit flags and asynchronous KV-cache recycling without heavy interpreter roundtrips: Allow registering low-overhead termination predicates directly within the vLLM scheduler loop. Provide efficient memory reclamation hooks to instantly free PagedAttention blocks for completed sequences mid-batch, avoiding dead compute cycles. Questions for Maintainers & Community Are there existing internal plans or hooks to handle asynchronous early-termination predicates inside the vLLM engine core without hitting Python GIL limits? What is the current accepted benchmark for evaluating per-step scheduling overhead in vLLM? We are currently profiling custom asynchronous volatile-flag checks and would like to share benchmarks if there is interest in contributing a PR. ### Alternatives _No response_ ### Additional context _No response_ ### Before submitting a new issue... - [x] Make sure you already searched for relevant issues, and asked the chatbot living at the bottom right corner of the [documentation page](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/), which can answer lots of frequently asked questions.

signal.text: ## Purpose Follow up on #51245 after the effective runtime fix landed in #51178. This PR focuses on simplifying deployment-wide data-parallel size ownership and adding a dense-DP regression test. - Store the explicit deployment-wide DP size only in `TransportMode::Bootstrapped`; `HandshakeOwner` derives it from `engine_count`. - Expose the deployment-wide value through `EngineCoreClient` and use it for `/get_world_size` and gRPC server information. - Remove the duplicate value and override path from server `Config` and `AppState`. - Move topology validation into the engine-core client so direct client users receive the same validation before sockets are opened. - Rename the Rust-only Ready field to `effective_data_parallel_size` while preserving the Python wire key with serde. signal.title: [Performance][MRV2] Use uint16 for penalty output counts
signal.text: ## Purpose MRV2 stores generated-token counts in a persistent `[max_num_reqs, vocab_size]` int32 tensor. When `max_model_len <= 65535`, each count fits exactly in uint16. This change: - uses uint16 counts for those configurations and keeps int32 for longer contexts; - pads odd vocab sizes so two uint16 counters can share one int32 atomic word; - casts counts to int32 before applying penalties. There is no API or sampling-semantics change. For Qwen3.5-9B with `max_num_seqs=256`, the count state drops from 242.5 MiB to 121.25 MiB. On an L40S, available KV cache increased from 18.86 GiB to 18.97 GiB, and KV capacity increased from 435,665 to 438,272 tokens. ## Not a duplicate - #47540 optimizes persistent penalty statistics in MRV1. - #49697 is a broad P800 MRV2 port with Torch fallbacks. - #34213 removes `expanded_local_pos` from the MRV2 penalty path. None compresses MRV2 output counts. ## Validation ```text /tmp/vllm-test-venv/bin/python -m pytest \ tests/v1/worker/test_gpu_penalties.py \ tests/v1/worker/test_gpu_input_batch.py \ tests/v1/worker/test_gpu_input_batch_v2.py \ --confcutdir=tests/v1/worker -v 25 passed in 22.29s ``` Ruff, Ruff format, mypy 3.12, typos, SPDX, filename, forbidden-import, `torch.cuda` API, and boolean-context checks passed. The GPU regression suite was rerun against main at `5c9ff536`. Qwen3.5-9B was also tested on an L40S with MRV2 explicitly enabled. Baseline and candidate returned the same text, finish reason, and token usage with presence, frequency, and repetition penalties enabled. A 100-sample GSM8K regression run showed no quality regression (0.87 vs. 0.88, with no invalid outputs). AI assistance was used for implementation and validation.

signal.title: Harden DeepSeek V3.2 fused kernel grids
signal.text: ## Purpose Harden the DeepSeek V3.2 fused Triton kernels against large single-iteration token counts. `fused_norm_rope` and the Triton fallback for `fused_q` placed `num_tokens` on CUDA grid-y. A launch with 65,536 tokens therefore exceeded grid-y's 65,535 block limit and failed with `Triton Error [CUDA]: invalid argument`. This change swaps the token and task grid axes so the unbounded token count is on grid-x. Token indices are promoted to int64 for safe address arithmetic. It does not change the kernel math or the CuTeDSL `fused_q` path. This does not duplicate an existing PR. Searches for the kernel names, DeepSeek V3.2 grid limits, and the 65,535/65,536 boundary found no matching open fix. PRs #52046 and #51915 touch the same kernel file but retain the affected launch grids. OpenAI Codex was used. ## Test Plan - Reproduce both Triton launch failures at 65,536 tokens on NVIDIA B300. - Add minimal public-API regression tests for `fused_norm_rope` and the quantized `fused_q` Triton fallback at the boundary. - Run the complete DeepSeek V3.2 fused-kernel test file on NVIDIA B300. - Run repository pre-commit hooks on the modified files. Model evaluation is not applicable because this only changes launch geometry and program-id mapping; the output computation is unchanged. ## Test Result - Before the fix, both launches succeeded at 65,535 tokens and failed at 65,536 tokens with `Triton Error [CUDA]: invalid argument` on NVIDIA B300. - `.venv/bin/python -m pytest tests/kernels/test_fused_deepseek_v32_norm_rope.py -q` - `52 passed, 14 warnings in 27.33s` - `.venv/bin/pre-commit run --files vllm/models/deepseek_v32/common/kernels.py tests/kernels/test_fused_deepseek_v32_norm_rope.py` - All applicable hooks passed. - `git diff --check` - Passed. ROCm hardware was not available for this test run. The modified Triton kernels are shared by the CUDA and ROCm DeepSeek V3.2 paths.

autotune round (`Tuning mxfp8_gemm: 100%|… 16/16`). - Exactly one rank of a TP pair then prints `Tuning mxfp8_gemm: 0%| | 0/16` for the next round; its TP peer never enters that round. - Both ranks of the pair sit in `futex_do_wait` (one at ~50% CPU, the peer at ~20%), GPU 0%. - All other ranks park at the barrier; EngineCore emits `shm_broadcast … No available shared memory broadcast block found in 60 seconds` once per minute forever. Startup never completes; no error, no traceback. The ranks desynchronize between tuning rounds, after which the cross-rank per-tactic timing collective blocks forever — one participant is inside the round-N profiling loop, the other never joined it. **Reproduction matrix** — the deadlock is independent of everything except the vLLM version: | vLLM | FlashInfer | NCCL | JIT caches | Result | |---|---|---|---|---| | v0.27.1 (official image) | 0.6.16.post3 | pip-bundled | warm | deadlock | | v0.27.1 (official image) | 0.6.16.post3 | system 2.30.7 | warm | deadlock | | nightly `dev18+g3d204dfda` | 0.6.16.post3 | system 2.30.7 | cold | deadlock | | nightly `dev18+g3d204dfda` | **0.6.17** (forced) | system 2.30.7 | warm | deadlock | | source build `dev54+gb96bcd0b4` | 0.6.18 | system 2.30.7 | warm | deadlock | | pre-#50892 build `0.26.1rc1.dev247` (Aug 2) | 0.6.17 | same | warm | **tunes clean** | The Aug-2 build uses the previous flow (distributed ⇒ tune on every rank, no process group, no cache broadcast) and completes the identical tuning workload on the identical hardware every time. **Workarounds validated on this cluster:** - `VLLM_FLASHINFER_AUTOTUNE_SKIP_OPS=mxfp8_gemm` — startup completes, but the un-tuned `FlashInferCutlassMxfp8LinearKernel` costs ~35% single-stream throughput (9.0 tok/s vs 14.4 tok/s tuned). - Patching `flashinfer_autotune` back to per-rank tuning (no `set_autotune_process_group`, no cache broadcast) — autotune completes on all 6 ranks and restores full performance (14.4–14.5 tok/s) on current main (`dev54+gb96bcd0b4`). Note: the synchronized flow already contains a mitigation for one hang trigger (`randomize_inputs=True` for EP ranks receiving no tokens) — this is a second, different trigger in the same design. I'll open a PR adding an opt-out env (`VLLM_FLASHINFER_AUTOTUNE_DISTRIBUTED_SYNC=0`, default keeps current behavior) that restores the per-rank flow for affected fabrics. ### Before submitting a new issue... - [x] Make sure you already searched for relevant issues, and asked the chatbot living at the bottom right corner of the [documentation page](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/), which can answer lots of frequently asked questions.
